The Ballroom at Buckingham Palace.—Since King Edward came to the Throne many great improvements have been made in the Royal Palaces. The ballroom at Buckingham Palace has been transformed with a view to avoiding the crush at such functions as the Courts, and State balls, and great things have been done in the way of re-clecoratine and improved lighting arrange- ments. All the walls and ceilinss are of white and gold, and the east proportions of the room enable dresses and jewels to be shown with much greater effect than in the Throne Room, which was generally overcrowded on occasions of State entertainments. The four new entrances to the bellroom are each nearly thirty feet in height, and proportionately wide. Each opening has four swing -doors covered with glittering mirrors on both sides, which, as they swing to and fro, throw out reflections Of the brilliant uniforms and the superb dresses and jewels of their Majesties° guests. Society Authoresses.—The Duchess of Buckingham has written a. story entitled " Penvala of the Black Watch," which she intends shortly to publish, Scottish tales, poems and plays appear to be favourite subjects with Society authoresses' and nmongst others who have devoted their literery tastes to such works are the Marchioness of Brerdalbane, the Countess of Cromartee, _Alm. Alfred Lyttletoneand Lady Betty Balfour. The Duchess of Bnckineharn's story gives a graphic picture of life in the Scottish Lowlands, on the banks of the Tweed. She writes with a thorough 'knowledge of the old Scottish dialect, customs and traditions, and her book is sure to meet With a favourable reception. Another Society authoress, the Countess of Dandonald, who has already appeared as a poetess, is said to he con- templating writing a life of Napeleon, her favourite study. Ponitry Farming as an occupation for Women.—lt is generally said that poultry keeping cannot be made to pay, but this occupation is included in a demonstration exhibition at Prince's Skating Rink, as affording an opportunity for girls, and a living witness to the practicability of the theory is adduced in the person of a lady who has been very successful with such an enter- prise at Gloucester. It does not however follow that because one lady has been able to show a profit, there- fore others will be able to do the same. She probably has speeial capabilities, and it may be that -If she had devoted herself to some other occupation she would have bean even more successful. Poultry farming has been tried by all sorts and conditions of men and women including not a few who have had ample capital. Being tired of town life and anxious to establish themselves in the country, these people have spared nothing to make the farm a success, yet they have failed almost without exception. To many people poultry farming on a small scale has afforded the means of supplementing their income to a limited extent, hut for aIl practical purposes it is not a very rash thing to say that this industry does not offer a reasonable prospect of success as a sole means of livelihood. The Gipsy Life.—Some of the most enthusiastic members of the Caravan Club are women, and the fore- gathering at Ockham, in Surrey, the first caravan "meet" ever held, reminds us that of late years, the idea of spending one's leelidav on a gipey outing has been growing in favour. All types of vans are used for this purpose, from the old-fashioned ,gipsy style to the "Pullman Car" horse and van, fitted with all possible modern improvements: Given fine weather, one can imagine that it is quite a pleasant way of passing the time, travelling twenty or twenty-five miles a day, and : putting up for the night on some wayside green, and in 1 a quiet meadow, hut the caravanner, like the yachts- woman, must be prepared for all weathers. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday before Messrs. Henry Roberts (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes and J. Mag,inn, Michml O'Malley, James-street, failed to answer to his bail on a charge of travelling from Earlestown to Warrington on the L. and N.-W. Railway on Saturday evening without paying his fare, and with intent to avoid payment thereof. It was explained by the clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White) that O'Malley was brought before the magistrates and remanded in order that the police might verify a state- ment he made with regard to the Earlestown police. He was allowed out on bail in his own surety, but had failed to put in an appearance. On Saturday night O'Malley arrived at Bank Quay Station, under the influence of drink, and without a ticket, having travelled from Earlestown. He refused to pay the fare or give his naive and address, remarking I that the police at Earlestown bad got his ticket. ' Edward William Dawson, ticket collector in the , employ of the L. & N.-W. Railway Company, said that at ten minutes past five on Saturday evening O'Malley ; came from off the platform and was risked for his ticket. He said he had not got a ticket, so the witness demanded I the fare. O'Malley replied that he would not pay it, but would rather have two pints. Witness than asked him for his name and address, which were also , refused, O'Malley replying " Yon will get nothing." ! He attempted to pass the barrier but witness prevented him. He used very profane and threatening language towards him, so he sent for the police and P.C. Leonard arrested him. , On being questioned the witness said that the man was making a rambling statement that the Chief Constable at Earlestown put him in the train. ; P.C. Leonard spoke to arresting O'Malley. He had since been to Earlestown to make enquiries concerning the statement made by the man anVound that Inspector Tones of the Earlestown police, had previously warned the man as to his conduct in Market-street,Earlestown, on Saturday. In order to get the man away the police promised to pay his fare to 'Warrington. When he was being taken to the station a motor accident occurred! and in the muddle the man's ticket was forgotten but he said he bad enough money to pay his fare. , Mr. H. Roberts: Is it customary for the police to • send undesirables from one district to another? Did the Earlestown police actually pay this man's fare In order to get rid of him? It is a most improper thing to do. Superintendent Monaghan: I have never heard of it , being done before. ! Mr. Roberts : It is not fair for the Earlestown police to get rid of him and send him into another district. I can't imagine how a Force could do such a thing. The railway company were perfectly right in • having him arrested. We fine him 103. including costs. We have taken into consideration the conduct of the Earlestown police who actually promised to pay his • fare to get rid of him and in all fairness they should pay this man's fine. If it had not been for these circum- stances we should have inflicted a very heavy penalty.

div.head: WOMAN'S IZEAT,M.
div.p: WOMAN'S IZEAT,M.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
IMPORTANCE OF MINOR DETAILS.

This is emphatically the day of small things in the world of Fashion, but it is just these small accessories to the toilet which make all the dif- ference, and mean so very much. A smartly-tied cravat that gives to a neutral-tinted gown just the right touch of vivid colour; a dainty chemi- Bette, in simple muslin, but finely tucked and spotlessly clean; a snow-white aigrette placed just at the correct angle (poise is everything in these matters)—these are some of the points which make or mar the success of many a gown.

div.head: SOME OF THE STLFFS NOW WORN.
div.p: SOME OF THE STLFFS NOW WORN.

Serge tissue is a good wearing stuff, dyed in many colourings; the cloths which the tailors delight in are of light weight. Stripes, herring- bone, weaving, and diagonal designs are all specially charming in chino effects. There is much originality, and bordered fabrics save expense in trimming, especially when accentuated by pip- ing and a touch of embroidery here and there; many of the soft silks rival the satins in their lustrous sheen. div.head: SOME VAGARIES IN MILLINERY.
div.p: SOME VAGARIES IN MILLINERY.

High and narrow crowns distinguish many of the French hats, and look very smart, especially with walking costumes. There is a marked change both in the height and width of the hats of to-day. The mushroom has disappeared, and the brim is of all widths. The Charlotte Cor- day crown remains with us, sometimes having brims of feathers. Coque and marabout trim. mings of vast size have grown so altogether vul- gar. declares the Queen, that they cannot but lose their prestige. Coloured Panarnas, Tuscans, and even Leghorns have been resuscitated. There are no bandeaus inside, and people wear some of them set back on the head bonnet fashion in a quite hideous style, Some of the hats are remarkable for the masses of feathers piled upon them, and the feathers stand out at right angles often as if they had no other con- nection with the headgear save that the top is sown to il. _

div.head: STRIPED COSTUME.
div.p: STRIPED COSTUME.

This smart little costume could be carried out in striped woollen material or linen. White striped with bright rose-colour would be very effecitive. The skirt has a double box-pleat clown the centre, the two side seams being wrapped over towards the back, and finished with stitch- ing and It uttons covered with rose-coloured
t eirecti

linen. The bodice is arranged in pleats to cor- respond with those on the skirt, and the but- tons are also repeated at each side- of the bodice. The square yoke is finished with a collar of the plain linen, cut with decided points at the cor- ners, and finished with a knotted ribbon of deep rose satin. The shoulder capes are cut on tho cross, and edged with a band of the, plain linen. The sleeves are gathered up the side seam, and finish with plain cuffs.

div.head: GOLOLJEED GLOVES.
div.p: GOLOLJEED GLOVES.

It is curious how little our shoes and our gloves change, remarks a Globe writer. Every year many novelties are put on the market, but it cannot be .said that they gain any great hold on the public taste, and on the subject Of gloves there is a rigidity of opinion which makes any startling deviation come almost under • the dreaded title of "bad taste." It is a pitfall, for instance,. to the inexperienced that in the daytime it is permissible, and in most cases even advis- able, that the glove should match the dress, but in the evening woo betide the rash experimenter i who appears n anything but white or cream kid or suede. A kind of tentative compromise 'has placed upon the market white gloves slashed with coloured kid, but these have not, so far, been very largely worn in ball-rooms. When they have appeared there, however, they have been rather successful. They are of the usual white kid up to the elbow, but just above the turn vandyked slashes of kid in the exact colour .of some part of the dress, usually the dominant part, are inserted to make a kind of gauntlet, or cuff. This makes the glove neat by keeping it in place. . _

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

POTATOES A LA HOLLANDAISE.—Scrape one and a-half pound of new potatoes of even size and put them in salted water containing the juice of half a lemon. Cook them carefully in fast-boiling water till nearly tender, then drain them in a sieve or cloth. Melt one ounce of butter, put in the cooked potatoes, and shake them over the fire for a few minutes. then add half a gill of ooenainei or wnitej sauce, and boil up. Cook for ten minutes longer, stirring gently so as not to break the potatoes. Mix the yolks of two eggs with a little milk or cream, stir, and pour over die potatoes, add a little lemon-juice, and servo.

OXYGEN AND PNEUMONIA.

Dr. N. H. Adams, Professor of Chemistry and Therapeutics in the Illinois Medical College, is quoted by the Medical Times as saying: "My experience with oxygen in pneumonia leads me to the belief that it is a valuable and often a necessary adjunct to the successful treatment of that disease. I can state with positiveness that it (1) relieves fast and laboured breathing, and thus rests the tired muscles, lessens the heart's work and conserves energy; (2) it slows and steadies a rapid and tumultuous heart; (3) it aids the elimination of carbon dioxide; (4) it is grateful to the patient.
"He is $
is no parson in camp, or I would send him. Make your peace with God." "Is there—no—hope?" he asked, feebly. "None." "But I must speak to you—tell you something before I die."
"Drink this," I said, holding a spoonful of port to his lips. "Now speak, and briefly, you have but little time."

" You," he said, slowly, "were a student when Maggie McLean—died. I know you. though you are altered. Sir, it was I who did the deed, not Burroughs—my passions mastered me when I met her—besides, I felt revengeful." . _ _ . _

Though I guessed as much before, this vil- lain's confession almost overcame me. Then I made a firm resolve. I would save this man; I would pluck him from the jaws of death if medil cal skill and nursing could effect this. But first I wrote out the confession, and in presence of two witnesses he feebly signed it.
At two o'clock the i-nan- was no worse. I never left his side for an hour all that day. I was nurse and doctor both.

At three next morning his life hung in the balance, but he rallied, and in three days' time he was out of danger—a prisoner now, and guarded by a file of Marines., We had almost reached Cripetown, when one morning I was summoned hastily from my tent about sunrise. It was to see Ogilvie—dead. Aye, dead enough. He had sprung on the sentry, wrenched the bayonet away,' and plunged it into his own heart. ,

Fred Burroughs returned to this eountry about the same time that I myself had a spell of leave, and was .soon established as florist and .seedsman in the little village on the Dee. And a sweet pee wife was Aggie DiteLolo. [Tar END.]

div.head: LIGHT OF THE MOON.
div.p: THE LIGHT OF THE MOON.

According to the results of a number of experiments carried out by two American scientists to determine ' the value of the moon's light, at its full phase our satellite's illuminating power is equivalent to 022 candle-power. At that phase, too, we receive nine times as much light as at half-moon, but, curiously enough, the moon is brighter at the phase between first quarter and full than at the similar phase between full and last quarter. The values are expressed in "candle-metres," and the expression "022 candle-power " means that the full moon illu- minates a whole surface to the same extent as a light equal to 0'22 candle-power would illuminate it from a distance of one metre. The candle used was made of amyl acetate,the diameter of the wick being eight milli- metres, and the height of the flame regulated to forty millimetres.

div.head: WANDERING MOLECUtES.
div.p: WANDERING MOLECUtES.

Even the most solid metals lose some of their molecules by dispersion from the sur- face, but some curious peculiarities are ob- served in the process of molecular disper- sion. For instance, when a piece of gold is pressed against a piece of lead, some of the molecules of the former dispense into the Lead. The process is, of course, extremely slow, and years are required before its effects become evident. But, slow as it is, the dispersion of the molocules of gold into a mass of lead takes place faster than into either air or water. The surface molecules of water disperse readily into air, but refuse to enter oil. The molecules of salt disperse quickly in water, but refuse to enter air, or most solids, in appreciable vantities.

div.head: SIZE OF THE SEA.
div.p: THE SIZE OF THE SEA.

This refers not to , the area of the oceans only, but to their total cubic content, which is reckoned by Edward A. Martin, of the Geological Society, at thirty times the cubic content of all the land lying above sea-level. In other words, if all the land of the globe were scraped off down to the level of the sea and thrown into the ocean, it would fill only one-thirtieth part of the enormous abyss which is occupied by the waters. According to Lyell, the mean height of the land above tea-level is I,oooft. whereas the mean depth of the ocean is 12,1000 ft. There are mountain peaks which rise as high above sea-level as the depressions of the ocean sink below it, but the average height of the land is slight compared with the average depth Qf the sea.

div.head: HOW A DOG KEEPS COOL.
div.p: HOW A DOG KEEPS COOL.

Professor Trouessart, of the Paris Museum of Natural History, in a lecture on animal heat, remarked that the dog, whose respira- tions in repose number only 25 Or 30 per minute, may in running acquire a rate of re- spiption as high as 330 per. minute. The effect of this acceleration favours the dissipa- tion of animal heat by evaporation from the pulmonary vesicles. The dog perspires iery little, or not at all, by the skin, pulmonary taking the place of cutaneous transpiration. It is this fact which enables the dog to pur- sue its game so long and persistently. Animals of the cat family, on the other hand, do not possess this peculiarity, and for that reason tigers, panther, and lions lie in wait for their prey, but do not pursue it over long distances. The bird possesses pulmonary transpiration in a very high degree.

div.head: BURIED MOUNTAINS.
div.p: BURIED MOUNTAINS.

lOne of the most remarkable features of the geology of a strip of north-west Scotland de- scribed in a recent memoir of the Geological Survey, is its ancient buried mountains. These mountains, carved out of the most ancient rocks of our land, ws;re submerged beneath the ocean, and buried in sand carried down by rivers. This sand now forms these great masses of red rocks known to geolo- gists as Torridonian, from Loch Torridon, where they occur in great force. These rocks have been themselves carved out into moun- tains, and the forces of denudation have re- vealed the fact that they have covered up more ,ancient mountains. Mountains are being buried in sand to-day in some parts of the world, though in a different way. In cer- tain parts of the great Asiatic deserts, and on the frontiers of India and Afghanistan, the wind heaps up the sand against the mountain. In some eases it is thus com- pletely covered.

A collection was taken on behalf of the Pan-Anglican Congress thank- offering.

Holy Trinity Church. Sermons on behalf of the day and Sunday schools were preached on Sunday, and there were large congregations at all the services. The Rev. H. A. Lester preached in the morning, and the children's service in the afternoon was conducted by the Vicar, (the Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton). In' the evening the preacher was the Rev. H. Norman, rector of St. Agnes, Birch, Manchester. Buckley-street Methodist Free Church. The Methodist Free Church, Buckley-streot, held its Sunday school anniversar, services on Sunday. There were good congregations in the morning and afternoon , whilst in the evening the Church was packed to over - flowing, many baying to stand. The preacher at all three services was the Rev. J. S. Hughes, and the chair- man in the afternoon was Mr. John Adams. The singing of the children all through the day was really splendid, and gave great delight to the congregations, and too much praise cannot be given to Mr. James Ryder the conductor, for the way in which he had trained the children. A feature of the afternoon and evening services was an action hymn by twelve little children, "The same Jesus." These little ones who had been instructed by Miss M. Plinston sang the hymn, and at the same time went through various poses to suit the words, and acted up to their parts with a delightful simplicity that charmed the hearts of every one present the preacher remarking in the afternoon that if it had been any other day, he felt sure that the congregation would have demanded an encore. Miss Plinston also noted as organist and accompinist throughout the day. Great credit is due to tho parents for the nice appear- ance of the children.

div.head: SUICIDE'S INSURANCE.
div.p: A SUICIDE'S INSURANCE.

£3,000 CL VIM AGAINST A COMPANY DISMISSED. i A judgment of importance to insurance companies . ' and to policy holders was given on Monday in the ;King's Bench Division by the Lord Chief Justice. I His lordship had reserved judgment in the case in i which Miss Fenny Joel, of Gosforth, Newcastle, the execntrix of the will of Miss Rosins Morrison, sued the ILaw Union and Crown Insurance Co., on a policy to I obtain £3,030 which the company had midertaiten to. pay on the death of Miss Morrison, When signing the company's proposal form, Miss Morrison stated that she had never had brain fever or any other disease of the brain, but after her suicide at the Empress Club in March 1906, it was found that nine I years previously, as a sequel to influenza, the insured lady suffered from acute ramis. -It was alleged that during a return of the trouble sho committed suicide. The Judge held that there was no fraudulent intent fon the part of Miss Morrison, but plaintiff could not recover under the circumstances, and the claim would be dismissed. As it was not a case of fraud he would, order the premiums to be repaid by the company.

div.head: WHITE ITY.
div.p: THE WHITE ITY.

One of the most interesting and novel processions ever seen in England passed through the principal streets of Manchester last Saturday afternoon, com- posed of the chief " exhibits " at the White City this sr-tson. Deansgate, Market-street, Piccadilly, Oxford- road, Stretford-road, right up to the gates of the White City—all these well-known thoroughfares were packed with people anxious to gain a view of the Red Indian Chiefs from the Wild West, the Bontoc Igorrates from the Phillipine Islands, the Millican Coons from the Southern States of America, and the many other interesting features which were part of the procession. When the gates of the White City were thrown open to the public shortly after one o'clock, thousands had lined - ; up waiting for admission, and the turnstiles were click- ing right through the afternoon and evening. The scene ;at the White City last Saturday evening almost baffles description, and it was almost impossible to believe One was really in the heart of smoky Manchester. Everybody appeared to be wrapped in amazement and admiration as they gazed around and saw myriads of electrio lights flashing all over the grounds. The bandstand streamed with tiny lights, and the fact that the world-renowned " Besses " occupied the" hoot" was sufficient induce- ment to attract many thousands. The Bontoe Igerrotes Village will undoubtedly be one of the greatest and most interesting exhibitions at the White City this season. During the past week hundreds of people have been flocking into the village watching these quaint people from the Phillipine Islands going through their ; war dances and primitive customs and industriee. The ' ever-popular figure 8 looks like beating all records this year, if one can judge Bona the manner in which visitors ;to the White City have packed the cars. 'Die gigantic scenic railway and water chute have also been in great demand, and slue to become extremely popular, as also will" Ye olde Mille." Among the many other side shows at the White City include" Hales Tours of the World," " Cleopatra ' the Egyptian Enchantress, " Millicans Plantation show of singers and dancers from ; Coonland."A thrilling exhibition is given by a young and plucky gentleman who is billed as" Dare Devil Watson." From a height of 50 ft. he dashes down a steep incline, ; and lands with a nerve shaking thud on the thick I matting prepared for his reception. Mr. J. Calvin 1 Brown is determined to make the White City the most up-to-date pleasure resort in England, and he has ; instructed his agents throuhgout Europe and America to obtain eveything of the very best in the' amusement world, and there is every indication that the ambition ' of Mr. Brown will be before very long gratified as the ; ambition of all who posress pluck, energy and deter- mination should be gratified.

div.head: ROYAL COURT MEATH. "Home, Sweet Home."
div.p: ROYAL COURT MEATH. "Home, Sweet Home."

As its title suggests, this is a domestic drama which appeals to the emotions and it has been well received by good houses this week. The author, Mr. Frank Lindo, who also plays one of the leading parts, has succeeded in weavinA a most interesting story, and there is a welcome absence of the far-fetched sensationalism which characterises too many dramas. The tone of the play is good and the audiences are -deeply touched by, the chequered fortunes of the young fisherman, Stephen Armitage, and his charming ulfe -Joan. To briefly outline the plot: Joan as a child was rescued from a wreck in which her mother perished and is brought up by David Armitage as his adopted daughter. The old salt cherishes fond hopes that some day Joan will wed his son, Stephen, and the first act sees the consummation $2 f his desire. The happiness of the young couple's married life, how- ever, is destined to receive a check. Gaunt paver'y N,sits the home and Joan, who has always had an linaseouptable yearning to move in higher circles, is inclined to retel. Just when matters are at their Worst, she learns that she is no less a r3rsonage than the daughter of the Duke of Ancaster. The fathe., who had thought his daughter was drowned at sea, overjoyed on accidentally finding that she is alive, and at once sends for her. She is persuaded to leave her husband and child, under the ia.p:ession that they will be well cared for, and to dwell " midst pleastu - and palaces," the pride of her father. But her co science troubles her, and to crown all she sees in a vision her child on the point of death, and a messenger from home brings the news that husband and little one are starving. This decides her to return to her lowly abode, and the ending of the play is as happy as anyone could desire. Miss Marion Wakeford figures 'with much success as Joan, her personal charms and high histrionic gifts eminently fitting her for the part. 11r. Frank Linclo gives a powerful version of Stephen Armitage and quickly wins the favour of the audience. Mr. D. Lawrence Doyle does well as the bluff old David Armitage and Captain Gerald Gambier is a dignified Duke of Ancaster. Mr. Helsby Wright as Lucas Llyle

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 23, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 23, 1908.
THE BLACKSMITH'S DAUGHTER.
BY VINCENT WRAY, Author of "Jacob Gunson, Agitator," "Tan. ners' Close," "The Folly of His Youth," "The khost of Starlight 'Abbey," Ste.

Amongst his fellow - villagers none was more popular—or more deservedly so—than Mr. James Ransome, the swarthy and muscular proprietor of the village smithy. And this, be it under- stood, despite a spice of pugnacity, which had a habit of asserting itself with aggravating fre- quency, and in a fashion that, to quote a Yankee- ism, considerably "riled" those who ventured to array themselves in opposition to "Jim's" strongly-expressed opinions. The blacksmith of Primrose Garth—as the charming picturesque spot in which he resided was called—was looked up to as a man of light and leading. Of course. he had his rivals for premier honours, the chief being the tailor and the shoemaker; but even, these, apart from the stormy passions of debate, and the meeting of the Parish Council—wherein there was always a sturdy struggle for pre- eminence -- generouely acknowledged that "Jim" was not without brains, adding the saving clause that, unhappily, he often enough failed to put them to good account. With his -" superiors" Ransome was not on the best of terms. The fact is that his views on many sub- jects were of an " advanced " type, and found little favour with the parson and the squire,. who, whilst they continued to patronise his smithy, never failed to impress him -with their opinion that he was a firebrand, and a very dan- gerous one, too, so far as his sphere of influence was concerned. . .

But, however divergent the verdict of the vi lagers as to,. Ransome's merits, there was only one opinion as to the beauty and virtue of his only child, Jessie. She was indeed ' the belle of Primrose Garth; and there was never a youth for miles around but at some time or other had sighed after as much as a favouring glance from her bright-blue eyes, or a word of encouragel- ment, be it ever so slight, from her tempting lips. Upon only one suitor did the fair Jessie smile, however. Walter Haydn—the envied one —was the only son of the reverend rector of the village. He was a fine, manly fellow, of whom his parents expected much, though at present he was only a 'barrister without a brief. The two had known each other as boy and girl; then, in the ordinary course of things, they were parted, he pursuing his studies at college and elsewhere, she looking after her father's domestic affairs. When again they met they had both arrived at the susceptible age, with the inevitable resalt that they fell in love with each other, promptly exchanged vows, and lost sight of the possibili- ties of parental disapproval, which not , uncom- monly troubles the course of true love. k / They had not long to wait for disillusionment. No sooner were the facts made known tch the re- spective parents than the eyes of the lovers were opened. The blacksmith, none too gently, gave his daughter to understand that he didn't want his girl to run after fellows who regarded them- selves as her betters. Let her marry in her own I station, and not seek to bring ridicule upon her I father. He believed in the people, not the classes. Of course, Jessie was every bit as good as the rector's son, but the rector didn't think so, and, in short, there was an end of the whole matter. On his part the rector was equally bitter. His son should never ally himself to the blacksmith's daughter; so much was certain. It was the height of madness, and not to be thought .of for a single instant. Thus it came about that young Haydn was bundled off to London with strict orders to forget his foolishness and try to make a mark in the world, whilst Jessie was sternly forbidden to "carry on " with. any more of her , moonshine and silly love-making." ; Three months sped on, and the two fathers congratulated themselves upon having nipped , the unwelcme business in the bud. Walter had ' protested that he would be true to his first love; ' Jessie was equally determined to marry no one else in the world. But after that neither spoke of the affair, which both parents soon came to I regard as forgotten and done with once for all.

The forge was silent. The anvil, stout and strong, lay idly in a remote corner, and not a glimmer reminded one of the rich red light that was wont to flash out at the bidding of the old, time-worn bellows. The forge was silent, yet all that day had big, patient horses, waiting to be shod, and anxious farmers whose ploughs had gone astray, lingered about the smithy door. There was a lot of grumbling. The blacksmith of Primrose Garth enjoyed a monopoly in his own line of business. It was many a mile to any sithar hillekamith'a ahrap am' flack -rorneely:;for the disappointed customers was to pour the vials of their wrath upon the head of the absent black- smith in the most vulgar and inelegant English they could command. "Where's Jim?" was the question that was on every lip, whilst the village lads inquired eagerly after the blacksmith's pretty daughter. "Anybody seen Jim Ransome to-day?" asked Garbutt, the shoeinaker, adding significantly: "I never know'd his place to be closed afore."

- "Yester e'en," broke in a big, raw-boned youth, "1 seed the smithy fire a-roaring like mad, and Jessie was standing just where I am now. I can mind it because I were thinkin' how bonnie she looked, and how—" "Here's parson," interrupted one of the group, which on hearing who was approaching became suddenly and respectfully silent. The Rev. Septimus Haydn paused when he reached the, assembled villagers. Then he glanced inquiringly round, and as no one ven- tured to explain the why and wherefore of the conference asked: "Is anything the matter, good people?" "Yes, sir," said Garbutt, doffing his cap, Jim Ransome's gone." "Gone? Gone where?" returned the rector, sharply. "I expect this is the outcome of his absurd notions., He was always a firebrand amongst us, and a peril to the good people (a favourite expression of the rector's) .of Primrose Garth. If I had had my wish he would have gone long since." " Ah, but you haven't your' wish," put in a strong voice. The Rev. Septimus turned very red, coughed violently, and, without venturing upon a rejoin- der, beat a hasty retreat, whilst the startled auditors turned to greet the missing blacksmith, Jim Ransome. " Wheres't thee been, lad?" queried Garbutt. "Here we've been waiting and wondering, and the•parson—" "Yes," replied Ransome, ungraciously, "ho has sore need to pray to be delivered from all uncharitableness, slander, and evil-speaking him- self." "But where be Jessie?" asked one of the vil- lage youths, with mor* than a shade of anxiety in his voice. "Ain't She come back along with thee?" • The blacksmith stared inquiringly at the speaker. "Jessie?" he exclaimed. "Jessie? Isn't she in the house?" • " No; she's gone, and nobody knows where." The rich red blood surged into the smith's swarthy face, and swelled the veins till they stood like 'whipcord on his brow. "What's thee mean?" he demanded. "Jessie not in the house? It's a lie—it must be a lie! She's not a girl to leave her father like this, to creep away as a thief in the night." Ho strode past the group, who gave way in silence, and watched sympathetically as he lifted the latch of his cottage door. The villagers re- mained expectantly' outside, waiting the black- smith's return; but he came not, and, as the shadows were beginning to steal around, they re- turned wonderingly and 'sadly to their homes. Meanwhile, Ransome entered his little front room, but no Jessie gave him friendly greeting. The fire had long since burnt itself out; the room had a dreary, desolate appearance that sent a cold chill through the devoted father's heart. Upon the table was a sheet of paper, carefully folded. The blacksmith opened it with ' trembling hands, and, as he read the contents, his rugged face grew strangely agitated. The big, burly frame shook with an all-powerful emotion, and, in his agony, the strong man bent and sobbed. Again and again he read the words that had so strangely moved him. But soon a change came over him. His fea- tures grew stern and hard, and he clenched his fists savagely as he muttered: "A poor man's lamb is lawful prey for the prowling wolf. It's the parson's son—it's Walter Haydn. May Heaven have pity upon him, for I will shew him none! Jessie has gone—she has gone; but one thing remains to me—a father's vengeance. The wolf shall not escape, even as the lamb, his vic- tim, did not. Look to yourself, Walter Haydn— look to yourself 1" And the next day the forge was silent still.

11. . James Ransome set out tond his daughter—' and Walter Haydn. Naturally, he first called upon the rector, who received him with scant courtesy; and when the blacksmith blurted out his belief that the girl had gone off with Walter Haydn waxed mightily wroth and indignant. "Nonsense—rubbish!" ho retorted, angrily. "The notion is monstrous, absurd, impudent. Do you think my son would so bemean himself as to elope with one of my parishioners? You may depend upon it that the girl's cleared off on some wild-goose chase." rtansome's lingers twitched nervously, and a menacing expression lingered upon his face; but, masteting the impulse to strike. the rector, he

replied, with a forced calmness: "Nay, sir; my girl's not that sort. There's only one thing that'd drive her from her home, and that's disgrace. Disgrace! Do you hear me?" and he brought his big fist down heavily upon the table in front of him. "Disgrace a thousand times worse than death. Oh that I had long ago laid her to rest beside her sainted mother in Primrose Garth churchyard! You are a father"—his voice sank into an earnest, pleading whisper—"if it were your daughter—' "Dear me, how you do talk!" interrupted the rector, with some show of indignation. "My daughter, indeed, as though such a thing were possible! Now, listen to me, Ransome. I'm sorry for you—from my heart I'm sorry. But why ever you should go flinging about charges such as you have brought against my house I can't for the life of me understand. Once for all, the thing's preposterous. Why, Walter's in London—"

Yes; tell me his address, and I will see him, ask him to answer me himself." "No, no, Ransome. In your present mood it is very undesirable that you should call upon him. I will write to him, and put the question bluntly; though, really, that is not by any means necessary. But you must not go—cer- tainly you must not," and the rector paced up and down his study floor in unmistakable agitation. "Then you refuse to give me your son's address?"

"Most certainly I do.V "Very well." The words were spoken quietly enough. "I will go to London, and if I have to tramp the city over I'll find him, and I'll tear the truth from his throat." The threat staggered the Rev. Septimus. He fairly reeled, panted, and when he had recovered himself the visitor had vanished. Still, upon re- flection, the blatlismith's words did not appear to mean much. London is a big place, and Ran- some's task was so stupendous as to be well-nigh impossible. At any rate, the rector had been forewarned, and he lost no time in putting his son upon his guard against the angry and sor- rowing father. In the heart of London, Ransome patiently and persistently pursued his search. He had never been there before, and in his ignorance of its vastness hc had thought that his purpose would be easily carried out, and the first stran- ger he encountered was considerably startled on hearing a long, elaborate description, first of Walter Haydn, then of Jessie. "Have you come across either of them?" asked Ransome, with feverish eagerness, and the poor fellow was deeply grieved when the stran- ger, broke into a low, mocking laugh. "Do you take me for a detective?" he in- quired, with a sneer, and, moving impatiently away, joined the endless procession of mortals that ever tamp up and down the busy streets. For days, foe weeks, the weary father sought and sought in vain. "London has no heart," he sighed, but would not give up the quest. It must not be supposed, however, that Ran- some had altogether severed his association with Prmirose Garth. He kept up a regular cor- respondence with William, the cobbler. Jessie might come home, he thought, and what would the poor lass do if she knew not where to find her father? Each night, on his return to the humble lodg- ings he had taken, Ransom° would take from his waistcoat pocket a crimpled sheet of notepaper, now ragged and torn, and sadly read Jessie's parting message. "DEAR FATHER," I fan leaving you; do net worry or grieve. It will be for the best. Some day I shall return, and you will be proud of me." _ . ' "

"Proud of you?" the blacksmith would mut- ter. "Proud of you? Nay, I can't never be that again. I must find you, Jessie. I must find you, and as for the scoundrel who—" But it was rarely that tlie sentence was completed. Always a frugal ma; Ransome had managed to put away a few pounds. "They'll be helpful to Jessie," he had thought, "when she gets wed." But the little pile was fast melting away. London is no place for cheap living. So he found employment at his trade, and worked and sought and sought and worked all through the live-long day and the shadows of the evening. But the money the blacksmith earned did not cover the expenses he entailed. 'lt is not pos- sible to travel about the big city without spend- ing money, and a good deal of it, too. In his straits, therefore, Ransome went to that last re- source of broken men—a moneylender. Always scrupulously honest in his dealings, he anticipa- ted no difficulty in raising a loan. He was soon undeceived. Of course, the shark—in this in- stance a Mr. Julius Benson—was willing to ac- commodate him at a high rate of interest, if satisfactory security was forthcoming. What security had the blacksmith to offer? Nothing— and yet, there was his place in Primrose Garth. Perhaps Mr. Benson would lend him money on that. Unsophisticated though he was, Ransom() knew it was of some value, since it was the only piece of freehold in the village. He Mentioned it to the moneylender, who accompanied him to Primrose Garth_to look over the property. They arrived at the village in the course 44-the---eftv, noon. Benson was satisfied, and proposed to ad- vance a sum of fifty pounds on mortgage. The blacksmith at once closed with the offer, and it was arranged that he, should call upon the moneylender a week later, when the transaction would be completed. Somehow or other Ransome fl as though he had committed a kind of sacrilege. For years out of., count the property had been in his family, and he almost expected to see his ancestors rise from their gravez in angry protest. Bitter as gall were his thoughts as he paced along one of the well- remembered lanes, All unwittingly he had taken the road leading to the Rectory. He was deep in sad thought, when a hand was placed upon his shoulder. He turned hastily round, and found himself face to face with the man he was seeking —Walter Haydn. For a moment he was so taken aback as to be unable to do more than gasp out: "Walter Haydn—you!" Then he turned on the .young man savagely. "Where's my daughter? Where is she, you scoundrel?" he hissed, fiercely. "I wish I knew," replied Haydn, earnestly. "Do you ,Aare to tell me that she is not where you have pk.`ced her? Disgraced—ruined?" Believe me, Ransome—" _ .

"No; I'll not believe you." Thu blacksmith lifted his powerful arm and struck the young man a violent blow. "Take that, you heartless villain," he shouted. Haydn clenched his fists, and then restrained himself. " You wrong me. I swear it," he said. "Were you not her father, I would have given blow for blow, strong as you are. Some day you will ask my forgiveness for this. I tell you—as you have sought for Jessie with aching heart, so have I. As you would give your life to save her, so would I. Great as IS your love for her, it is not greater than mine." The young fellow spoke earnestly; to any other listener, at least to a disinterested one, his words must have carried conviction. But Ransome be- lieved him not. "I shall find her," he said. "I shall see her agairt; and, as true as there is justice in . the heavens, if you are lying to me, as I feels in my soul you are, I will strangle the breath out of your miserable carcase. No, don't speak, lest now and hero I--" .

_ He could not, such was his rage, complete the sentence, and, without another word, he turned away. Of course, during his brief stay in Prim- rose Garth he encountered many of his old friends; but they found him strangely altered, and not a few were of the opinion that his trouble had turned Jim Ransome's brain.

The months sped on, and still there was no news of the missing girl. The smith's appear- ance changed greatly: A rough, thick stubble was allowed to grow upon the broad, thick-set chin, the face had lost its vigorous aspect, and the giant form was woefully bent. Ransom° had had to visit the moneylender again, and that, gentleman took good care that he got' the blacksmith in his clutches. Julius Benson had his eye on the property in Prim- rose Garth. The squire, he knew, would gladly buy, it, and for a comparatively big price, too. Accordingly, Shylock made it his business 'to swoop down upon his clieht for the 'return of the money advanced, s.ervtd• him with a process, and when the wretched man admitted his in- ability to satisfy the demands of the rapacious bloodsucker proposed that, to save extra legal expenees, he should dispose of his property, upon which, as Benson reminded him, he held a mortgage. The ' blacksmith was well-nigh distracted. "Wife dead, daughter gone, home passing from me," he muttered. "Nothing is left to me— nothing that is worth living for."

The Shakespeare had once been a flourishing hall of minic. but, as newer and more commo- dious buildings sprang up around, it seemed destined to perish in the keen struggle for exist- ence. It was Mr. Julius Benson's financial genius that retrieved 'it from the decay into which it was rapidly falling. He bought the 1 structure for the proverbial "old song," formed' a new company, and then looked about to find new attractions which should draw and hold the public, and thus bring a shower of shekels into the pockets of the shareholders. He succeeded in his quest, as he succeeded in most things. The attractiort he discovered was a young singer of surprising beauty, and gifted with a voice of uncommon purity and power. " Marie Maynard," the bills announced, when he considered her ready for a first appearance, "is the most lovely and accomplished artist eves introduced to the British public." On the strengtn ox this assurance, cleverly emphasised by 'inspired" paragraphs in the newspapers, a crowd of eager, novelty-loving pleasure4seekers hammered at the doors of the Shakespeare long before the hour that they were timed to open..

Ijulius Benson's anticipations were more than fulfilled. The British public, or that portion of it which frequented places of amusement, were in raptures over the new star. "She sings divinely," they said, in boxes and dress circle. "She's a reg'lar topper, a treat," was the ver- dict of the pit and gallery. Of course, Mr. Benson was hugely delighted. "She's fixed by her engagement with us for three years, and *illy receives two pounds a week," he said to his brother directors. "The Shakespeare is made." "How did you manage to secure her so cheaply?" asked one of the other directors. "Oh, she's from the country; innocent, you know," replied Benson, with a-chuckle. Time passed on, and Mario Maynard's fame shewed no sign of fading. On .the contrary, her hold on the public grew stronger and more certain. Of course, she received offers of engage- ments elsewhere, but Benson's agent had fastened her. She was not her own mistress.

I It was a eoldw inter's night in December. The snow had fallen heavily ; but the pavements and roads of London persistently refused to allow it to rest, even for an instant, upon their bosom. A cold, piercing wind, wet ground, and air filled with the fast-falling flakes made the night air as comfortless as it well-nigh could be. But the patient, all-suffering public are not to be spoilt of their entertainment. Marie. Maynard was to appear with a ne* song, and the capacious hall was crowded from floor to gallery. The first " turns " were not out of the com- mon, and failed to provoke the enthusiasm of the audience; a low, continuous hum of conversation drowned the efforts of the artists. After the in- terval, a silence, deep as death, fell upon the as- sembly. Opera-glasses were levelled at the stage from every part of the house, and, as , Marie Maynard advanced to the footlights, a spontaneous cheer burst from the expectant audi- ence. They had excellent taste, indeed! Tall and shapely, with long masses of light brown hair that hung untrammelled round her beautiful head, Marie Maynard might well be the envy of , her sex, and the admiration of all. And her voice ! Its deep, thrilling richness, its wonderful power were well-nigh indescribable. Little , wonder was it that the Shakespeare was proud ; of its "star" artist. She commenced •to sing; ' but scarcely had she given a dozen notes when, I suddenly, a voice rose out of the pit—a voice whose every tone spoke the pent-up agony of long grief and weary waiting. It is she—my Jessie! 1 have found thee ! " Before he could be prevented, the blacksmith of Primrose Garth had sprung upon the stage, amidst a wild storm of hisses and similar marks of popular derision and anger. "lie is mad; seize him I Save the girl! " cried the indignant audience. But the cry died away upon their lips, as they saw the beautiful singer throw her arms round the rough in- truder's neck—and then they wondered. The curtain guickly descended, and the mem- bers or the directorate who were present hastened to the back of the stage to learn what had happened. "Are you going on with your song?" asked Julius Benson, as soon as the relationship be- tween the two had been explained. " I am tired, father," • said Jessie, "I am tired; take me home."
But. nevertheless. Marie Maynard sang -every other evening in that week. Her father told her of his financial difficulties; and to Mr. Benson she said:

"I will sing for this week if you will agree to relieve my father from his liabilities." Vainly did Benson beg. expostulate, and threaten. Jessie was firm, and he had to submit. The engagement she had entered into could not have been enforced in a court Of law.

Jessie, it was explained, had been taken to London by Benson's agent, who had come across her while staying in the neighbourhood. She promised to leave home secretly, as soon as opportunity offer&l, and upon her father's" de- parture to Ironville—whither he had been sum- moned for reasons associated with his business— she met the agent, und was driven to the nearest town, from which they were soon whirled away to the big city. " You will make your for- tune," he declared, "and your father shall share it with you." Ransome told the girl of his meeting with Walter Haydn. and how he had accused him of spiriting her away. You owe him an apology," was the reply. "And he shall have it,' replied the black- smith, heartily.

The smithy was soon busy again, the anvil stood in its appointed place; and the fire blazed and the bellows roared, and many a wayworn traveller would pause outside tho forge, amazed to hear a voice so beautiful and so perfectly- trained in such a place. But, if report speak truly, the smithy, and Primrose Garth, too, will soon lose the singer. Walter Haydn has claimed compensation for the blacksmith's assault on him: and he has got it. "Jessie is thine, lad," he said, "though I don't like parting with her again. Maybe, though,— he d "tha parson won't agree, and then---" But the reverend rector has surrendered; albeit, he is not over well pleased to think that Liz son's future wife is a blacksmith's daughter.

TIIE SCOTTISII NATIONAL EXHIBITION.

The suggestion to hold a Scottish National Exhibi- tion in Edinburgh this year originated amongst the ramoters of the very successful Exhibition held in the Meadows in 18Sti. Considerable impetus was given to the movement by the concession from the Edinburgh Corporation of the use of the Saughton Hall Estate,and by their liberal contribution to the Guarantee Fund, an example happily followed by the other Cities and principal towns in Scotland. This practical interest, and the inclusion in the list of patrons and guarantors of the leading names from all ranks of society, justified the executive claiming for the exhibition a truly Scottish National character. Its aims and scope are, however, of a far wider and more comprehensive nature than merely Scottish, for there is exemplified all that is best in Art, Science, Literature and Industry from His Majesty's Dominions all the world over,tind it is therefore a National Exhibition in the widest sense of the term.

The buildings have been erected from designs by Messrs. Walker and Ramsay, architects, Glasgow,whose piens were selected from a large number of competitive schemes by the Assessor, Mr. J. G. Burnot. The main erections are the Palace of Industrieq, the Machinery Flail, the fine Art Galleries the Music end Conference Hall, the Winter Gardens, the Welcome Club, the Prince's Restaurant, the Canadieu Pavilion, Van Houton's . Cocoa Pavilion, &c . . . . - • •• • •

The Palace of Industries the most striking and most expansive building of the series. It covers an area of 100,600 square feet. The structure has been built of timber, and the outside walls are covered with fibrous plaster, and the er€3tion is of a white and attractive appearance, nicely ornamented Ina total cost of this structure amounted to £10,340. The arrangement of stalls forms a central avenue east and west, a main avenue north and south, and six groups, accommodating exhibits of an exceptionally high-class character, com- prising the following sectioLs :—Scottish, English, Irish, Dutch, Javanese, Italian, and Canadian besides sections devoted to Education, Transport and Women's Work. _ .

• The exhibits in this hall comprise a number of inter- esting features, such as printing, lithography, shipping, mining, electric, gas, steam, water, sea _ge disposal, baking and confectionery plant, the majority of which are working, and thus providing a corsiderable degree of interest for the visitor. The fine art galleries undoubtedly form one of the special features of the exhibition. The materials used in their construction are light stc3l frames coated with fibrous plaster to form the walls, which intnnally are lined with asbestos from the roof to the foundation at a cost of £3,075. The nine large galleries into vihich this building is divided house col lectiors of purely Scottish Art by the best-known painters, as well as a collection of rare and historic exhibits that must app3al t 3 evely Scotsman, and should prove at the same time intensely interesting to visitors from all parts of the world. The photo- graphic section is also pat Lioularly interesting, and well worth a visit. It will be found in the same gallery. , The collection of pistols and claymores that played a part in the Ja?,obito rising is am y interesting, as also are a number of rings cont -..ining locks of Prince Charlie's hair. Two famous brooches are on view. The one known as the Ballochyle brooch was at one time used as a charm against the power of witches and for the curing of diseases in man and beast ' • the other brooch is that said to have been given by Robert the Bruce to the ancestor of the present owner, Captain Mac Neal, Ugedale, Ca mpbelltoa n. The Music and Conference Hall is the most striking building of the series. It is circular in shape, with prettily decorated outside walls, and the roundness is relieved by four Ornamental Towers, which are utilised to give access to the gaiter/ inside. Internally the structure is 100 feet in diameter and 40 feet from floor to ceiling. Its cost was £4,997, and it a2,commodates upwards of 2,000 people. A striking novelty in the shape of a 'fairy fountain " occupies the centre of the Hall. _ _ _

The Winter Garden is of a permanent character, and will be available for the use of the citizens of Edinburgh after the Exhibition is over. It covers a space of 3,000 squire feet, and is built of iron and wood lined on roof and walls with glass, and after the Exhibition will be a conservatory on a huge scale. A sum of nearly £l,OOO has been spent on this structure. Canada has erected a special pavilion for the display of her wares, and, as usual with our enterprising Colony, the imilding is a handsome one. I The Small Holdings Buildings Wiibit comprises a I complete homestead for a 20 acre farm, designed by Mr. ' Inglis, and premiated by the Royal Highland and Agricultural Society. A number of premiated plans are exhibited on the walls of the d selling-rooms, and form a practical solution of one of the live problems of the day.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

S.turday brought Warrington no better luck and the Ithird match of the season, which was the first League engagement, resulted in another defeat. St. Helens was the scene of operations and last year's champions - showed that they have lost none of their form for they triumphed by a majority of 40. Going in first, St. Helens amassed 105. The wicket was on the slow side and runs were always registered with great difficulty,so that the individual scores were not high, L. Hammill- (2o) being the top contributor.

Warrington made a bad start, J. C.llon being taken in the slips with only a couple of runs on the score sheet, making way for T. Wright. W. Richardson put up a splendid defence and Wright played the bowling with rare confidence. At 22; however, a misunderstand- ing cost Wright his wicket, after he had knocked up 14) and folloaing this disoster Warrington were always fighting an uphill battle. At 22 W. H. Podmore spooned one to Marsder. which was safely helc. and seven runs later another double disaster befel the visitors, for after Richardson had been given out at 15—a doubtful decision —Cresswell was taught, so that half the side were out. W. V. Turton stayed rntil 40 runs were registered and then Holden bowled him. The Warring- ton captain, B. Silock, was playing a splendid game to save his side from defcat, whilst J. 'Thompson gave promise of a fine innings. At 52 the lest-named was held by Rigby, and the end was now speedily in sight, for after Holden had bowled Dolan, H. Callon shared a , similar fate. Duckworth whipped in and forced a ' boundary stroke and was then caught, the innings closing for 65. Mr. Silcock took out his bat for a patiently-played innings of ten, and it is but just to say that the St. Helens bowlers were considerably assisted by the state of the pitch. The fielding of the Warring- ton side was very smart.

Warrington second are doing great things. They administered a very severe drubbing to St. Helens 2ad on Saturday, amassing 101 against the visitors insigni- ficant total of 14. Partridge was the top scorer for Warrington with 23, whilst Thewlis captured six wickets for 8 runs and Sennett three for 5.

In the Warrington and District League, Bewsey Wesleyans tried conclusions with the "Guardian "Office and registered a victory by 11 runs. J. Armitage, who knocked up 14 in fine style, was the only batsman to reach double figures.

Cheshire Lines Engineers accounted for Wilderspool Brewery with 14 runs to spare. The top score was forthcoming from the losing side, R. Hallows compiling 25. For Engineers E. Deeley gave .a creditable display for his 18 not out and J. Duckworth made a useful 15.

A junior league encounter between St. James's and Warrington Excelsiors resulted in a hollow victory for the Saints, who piled on a majority of 78.. For the winners H. Fleming batted well for his 29 runs, and L. Walker bowled effectively, taking four wickets for tire rurtg.

Not a solitary scorer in the Sankey v. Orford match attained double figures and there was a grand array of "ducks." The feature of the game was the bowling of Jolley who accounted for all the Sankey wickets but one and accomplished the" hat trick."
There was an exciting struggle between Marshhouse- lane and kloly Trinity, the first-named being victors by a single run. Bramball batted in fine style for his 16 and Taylor bowlcd well.

Warrington Commercial Travellers are evidently doughty cricketers and on Saturday they accounted for their fellow knights of the road at Birkenhead by G 5 runs. A. E. Walker was in brilliant form with the bat and ran up the bendsome score of 54.

Monk's hall and Cots eleven entertained Haigh and had the bad luck to be beaten by 7 runs. J.Seddon (13) was the winners most successful batsman, but not one of the home players reached double figures.

Latchford Baptists visited Moore and inflicted defeat on the villagers by 29. J. Conway was largely respon- sible for the victory for in addition to bowling with deadly effect, he knocked up 22 not out.

Walker'i Brewety had no difficulty in recording a victory at The expense of Winwick Asylum, their majority being 44. For the winners H. Cook and E. Allen batted well, H. Cook making 30 not out. W. Norman bowled splendidly, taking six wickets for as many runs.

Sankey Wire Mills 2nd and Platt Bridge Independent Methodist 2nd were well matched, but the Wire Mills claimed the victory by 6 runs. P. Bladen (18) N\ es their top scorer, but his efforts were surpassed by G. Walker who made 25 for the losers.
There was another close encounter between the Secondary School and St. Mary's, the last named being victorious by 3 runs. J. Dolan (12) was the top scorer.

Grappenhall fared badly at Knotty Ash, the home team triumphing by 64 runs. For the winners S. W. smith made a splendid 43, and H. E. Barley captured seven wickets for 17 runs. Ilutchins made the best batting display for Grappenhall, his innings realizing IS. -- Latchford easily defeated Brunswick (Runcorn) by CO to 27, Bennett taking seven wickets for 12 runs and P. Grice scoring 17.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The first round of the Warrington Works Bowling Competition was continued on Saturday when the following teams met on the Liverpool-road ground : Orford Tannery and Longford Wire Works, Monks flail and P. and K., Robertson's and Whitecross No. 1, Rylands's No. 1 and Fletcher's No. 2.

The match between Orford and Longford was of an exceedingly interesting character, Orford. winning by 140-139, thus leaving the small margin of seven points. The opening stages of the match were rather tame for J. Melbourne handsomely defeated J. Gleave by 15-4. The most interesting game was that between H. Atherton and M. Cunningham. Operations opened in the former's favour and continued so until the twentieth end, when the game was 11-11. Cunningham then got a single but Atherton again drew level and afterwards scored a point. Cunningham then registered a couple of points, thus winning by 15-14.

11Inch need not be said about the match between Rylands's and Fletcher's, for Rylands' won every game which gave them the splendid majority of 93 points. The only close encounter was that between G. Shaw and W. Wnitefield, the former winning by two points.
Roberton's were severely 1 trounced by Wbitecross No. 1, the latter being victorious by 180-50. Whitecross won all the games, the highest score agairst them being nine.

The encounter between Monks Hall and P. and K. was la ;king in excitement for P. and K. were victorious in all the games with the exception of three. D. Smith (Monks Flail) could not fiaci his form and was soundly defeated by D. Gibson to the extent of fifteen points to one. It seemed as if Monks, Hall were discouraged by this bad opening for they made a poor show all through and were defeated by 161-108. One of the most interesting games was that betwe n Rosterne and Thomason. Thomason gained the lead at the beginning but at the third end Ito.t.rne got ahead of him but not to stay, for at the eleventh end his opponent gained the lead which he maintained until the end, and triumphed by 15-11.

R. Wilcock looked RS if he was going to defeat J. Hill at the commencement for he led all the way up to the fourteenth end when the players drew level at 10-10. Hill then got a couple of points and finally rau out winner by 15-13.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

That the popularity of the Warrington Club is in no way diminishing is evidenced by the splendid musters which continue to turn up for the various functions week after n-csk, On Saturday last the members made their initial incursion into Loncsshire, Hunt's Cross being the rendezvous. Between 20 and 30 wheelmen took part and the weather being all that could be desired from a cycling point of view, a most enjoyable run was the result. After an excellent tea the majority of the members indulged in their favourite pastime on the pretty little grcsn attached to the Hunt's Cross Hot al.

Tuesday evening found only a bare dozen carrying out the mid-week fixttre to Little Leigh, operatic practice claiming a number of members. The advisability of changing the practice to some more convenient night, so as not to interfere with the club runs is bein g seriously considered.

There was again an excellent turn-up at Sankey on Wednesday evening, where almost 30 members could be seen putting on the finishing touches preparatory to the commencement of the Cup Competition a week hence.

To-day the club pay their first visit of the season to the Forest of Delatnere, the Abbey Arms being their headquarters and given a continuance of the present weather another large gathering of members is sure to be found at this charming EWA} Which i$ just now looking at its host.

IT is to be regretted that THE "SCIENTIFIC" on his retirement from the BASIS, groat post which he filled in Egypt with so much credit and public advantage Lord CROMER did not enter the House of Commons instead of the House of Lords. He is a really first class fighting man in the cause of Free Trade, and speeches delivered to the Peers on that, as on most other subjects, are to a large extent thrown away, for they are most indifferently reported, whereas the speech delivered by Lord CROMER on Wednesday deserved not only to be reported in full, but also to be distributed to every English house- hold. The DUKE of 111.taLBOROUCIII had a curiously indeterminate motion, the object of which was to call attention to the recent changes which have been made in the tariffs of the self-governing Colonies for promoting their economic develop- ment and the extension of their trade relations with ths united Kingdom and foreign countries, and to the desirability of increasing the productive power of the Mother-Country and the Empire as a whole by the arrangement of reciprocal preferences It was entirely a question-begging resolution. But the more we have of these in either House of Parliament the better, if their effect is to produce such smashing speeches as that of Lord CROMER. We are invited to adopt " a scientific Tariff," said the late administrator of Egypt. What did that mean ? Australia has recently been engaged in an attempt to increase its revenue by placing its taxation on a " scientific" basis. 119 proposed to draw the curtain aside and show the scientific tariff men at work in their laboratory. They had, of course, extremely difficult and complicated questions to deal with, as was inevitable. They dealt with them in a manner which showed that their " science " was of a some- what abstruse character. Then Lord CROMER went on to expose as remarkable a system of taxation of foreign produce—by which phrase the produce of the Mother-Country is chiefly indicated—as is to be found anywhere in a rather tariff-ridden world. We select one from the many examples with which ha amused and astonished his brother Peers. It refers to writing materials, but mainly to such as are used in schools. Now, writing materials, if they consist of pencils and wood, are admitted free ; but if they have metal caps they are subject to a tariff on that account. The pencils must be perfectly plain, however, if they are to get through any sort of trapdoor in

the tariff-wall. If they can be described as fancy pencils, they are liable to a duty of 25 per cent. That is one of the subtle distinctions made by the scientific tariff. Here is another, still referring to the same objects of scientific taxation. If a school- master orders from abroad a box of pens and pencils—a mixed consignment, that is to say—he pays no import duty, but if he orders pencils without pens he has to pay a duty of 25 per cent. Why this is so we cannot say. Nobody can. These curious arrangements and strange dis- tinctions are made in relation to every branch of every industry. That is necessarily the case where a Protective tariff is in existence. In France, for example, the collectors of Customs are instruct° d in their duties by volumes which almost approach to the dimensions of an Encyclopedia, and which have much of the character of that kind of publication. Under iron, for instance, there is a definition of that metal, followed by a great number of sub-definitions. The collector has to real extensively in order to acquaint himself with the amount to be charged on iron in this or in the other state. Otherwise. like the English railway porter, he might get into the confused state of miad which resulted in the declaration that " turtles is insects." It all means, of course, the creation of a great official class of wholly, unproductive persons,living on the produce of the industry of others. It is probable that in Australia the collection of the tariffs costs fully one-half as much as the tariffs produce, and this, let it be observed, is what is called " scientific taxation.
Saturday's horse .parade THE Honsu PARADE. was a distinct credit to

Warrington. It may have been lacking in picturesqueness, but in the chief essentials it was admirable, and one heard nothing but expressions of admiration from the crowds of spectators who assembled. On recalling the first parade eight years ago, one cannot but be struck by the immense contrast. It has been a case of progress all along the line, and from ' small beginnings the parade has obtained dimen- sions of which any town might be proud. I But, most gratifying of all, the quality has improved many-fold. The object of the promoters —to encourage the best possible treatment of the horses by their owners and drivers—is being surely attained and each year sees an improvement. If ever an institution has fully justified its existence it is the Warrington Horse Parade and we hope its work will be more and more successful as years go by. The " public v. brewer" Mn. DODOS & Cor.oxur, struggle is getting some- HALL WALKER'S what tame as a combat. LAMENT. Our friends the brewers made a very bold show to commence with, but their bristling guns on closer acquaintance turned out to be " dummies" and in no way capable of making any reply to the red-hot shot poured in by the temperance reformers. Their shells, being largely gassy, burst harmlessly, and for some time " cease fire " seems to have been a standing order in the enemy's quarters. An occasional venture- some foeman strays into the fire zone, only however to be quickly pulverised. Last week Colonel Hall Walker RP., cast a bomb of the customary type among the Widnes Conservativ3s. It created little alarm, thoegh the gallant colonel predicted that if the Licensing Bill became law " he should cease to be their member, probably have to soli everything he possessed and start afresh in life." This dire prediction of personal ruin has tempted Mr. James Dodds to examine the balance sheet of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Limited, "to see what chance there was of the colonel having anything left," as he told the audience at Sankey on Monday. He finds that the profits of the Walker Companies for 1907 amounted to the nice comforting sum of £326,461 in addition to the balance brought forward from the previous year of £16,905. Roughly speaking a million pounds of capital is held in ordinary shares, mostly by members of the Walker family, who receive a dividend of 10 per cent. In addition there is a reserve fund of over half a million pounds, so that Colonel Hall Walker must be the gloomiest of pessimists if he can con jure up visions of all this security vanishing into thin air merely because one-third of the country's licences, aod the monopoly value of the others, are to be surrendered to the State at the end of 14 years. Mr. Dodds also very properly pointed out that the whole of this vast capital value would have to be irretrievably lost before the widows and orphans, for whom the brewers profess such tender care, could be pecuniarily endangered. The brewers' case is indeed in a parlous state when the last resort turns out to be " crocodile tears" from millionaires who still entertain hopes of winning the Derby.

Lord Egerton of Tatton and CHESHIRE LAND- the Duke of Westminster LORDS AND THE have both given notice tO Saloom. the Cheshire Education Committee that in the event of the present Education Bill becoming law they will resume possession of the schools which they own. The Lord of Tatton has already given notice to the managers of Rostherne school and Egerton school to quit the school premises in March next. At its meeting on Monday the Education Committee decided upon the erection of Council schools in the districts concerned. BY taking this course the Committee returned the right answer, and as time goes on the same answer will be returned all over the country to private owners or trustees who demand that the public school shall be their school to convert into an annexe of their Church or do as they like with. ' The text of the letter from the Duke of West- minster's estate agent to the Education Committee is worth reading : I am desired by his Grace the Duke of West- minster to inform you, as clerk to the Cheshire education authority, that, owing to the legislative proposals now before Parliament, he has instructed me, as his agent, to give notice on the proper daY . to the managers of some eight schools in his owner- ship to terminate their agreements, with the inten- • tion, if the Bill becomes law, to resume possession of the school buildings. I am further desired to state that his Grace has at all times been willing that facilities should be granted for children to recei-,e the religious instruction desired for them by their parents ; as, however, the schools were • built by his predecessors as Church of England schools, he could not submit to their being appro- priated by the State under the conditions laid doWa by the Bill before Parliament. We cannot help thinking that the average citizen, irrespective of party, will feel ashamed that it should be in the power of anyone, duke or no duke, to write and act in this way. The Duke's legal rights are indisputable ; he can do what he likes with his own—his own building. What we should remember is that it is the community which pro- vides every penny of the money wliici maintains , tho school carried on in the building. But whether it be now, or five years hence, or ten years hence the conclusion of this controversy is certain. Every year the number of children in Council schools and undenominational schools increases over the number o! children in denominational schools, and as the sentiment for education increases it will seem intolerable that the natural growth of the public system should be barred by the order of a landlord, or a clergyman, or the existence of an old-fashioned schobl building and a traditional claim to occupy the ground. We wish the change to come peacefully and with due regard to religious education ; but come it will, in one way or another, and the Church must seriously consider whether any time is likely to be more favourable for a settlement than the present.

The stamp orator had ta-ken his stand in the centre of the square, and opened his harangue A small number of listeners stood about twenty yards away, and as new-comers arrived they all kept at this reapectful distance, until the speaker was surrounded by a large but thin circle of an audience. Try as he would, he could not attract anyone to come nearer. A wag who was passing took in the situation, and called out in an agitated voice, "For Heaven's sake, give the poor fellow air! "

Wisdom lies only in trutli— Goethe. Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise.— Gray. , The pursuit of perfection is the persuit of sweetness and light. —Matthew Arnold. Nothing in the world is so cruel as the tender mercies of a real philanthropist. —Sir 'William
Harcourt. Nothing that is necessary shocks really sensible people.—Crawforci. There is no penalty to virtue ; there is no penalty to wisdom.—Ernerson. . .
Time, whose tooth gnaws away eyprything else, is powerless against truth. —Huxley. " Let your light so shine before men that they see " —not what is going on behind it.—/I. B. Sheridan.

Lives are made i;eautiful and sweet By self-devotion, and by self-restraint—Longfellow. * * * The annual meeting of the Football Club on Thurs- day evening was on the whole a harmonious and satis- factory gathering. Members assembled in their hundreds and took a keen interest in the proceedings. What little discord there was seemed to come from some few members with more ideas lhan discretion in regard to club management. Full confidence was shown in the officers and committee by their re-election with substantial majorities over other competitors. The Club has been well-managed during the past season, as the sound financial state of the club testifies in the face of lessened gate receipts. With better luck in the season to come—nearly every player was injured last winter—the Club should stand an excellent chance of gaining further honours. Even yet they are the only Lancashire Club to have won the Northern Union Cup ! And their motto is "Excelsior."

* * * Congratulations to Alderman Tinnion, J.P., on his unopposed election to the presidency of the Warring- ton Football Club. It is no small honour in theso days to attain to this position for the Club has over a thousand members and is undoubtedly a power in the land so far as football is concerned. Alderman Tinnion has been connected with the Club continuously for thirty years originally as a player and since as a member, and subscriber. No one can suggest, there- fore, that he has been hastily thrust into the position he holds to-day. He takes the place of a contemporary in Dlr. J. E. • Warren, who has been even more prominently identified with football than Alderman Tinnion. The good things said of Mr. Warren on Thursday we have no doubt will be fully applicable to Alderman Tinnion a year hence. * * * There was no dissentient voice in either House of Parliament on Monday to the motion providing for the erection, at the public expense, of a monument to Sir Henry Campbell- Bannerman. M. Balfour was I happily well enough to be in his place and to be as 1 eloquent with his tongue as he had already been in his recent letter to Mr. Asquith. Mr. John Ilbdnaond is always admirable on these occasions. Parliamentarians recollect the excellent taste in which, while not divid- ing the House, he stated that he could not support a memorial to Lord Salisbury. On Monday ,his task, less delicate, was equally well performed. We must quote one passage : This statue which is about to be voted will be erected at the expense of the people of these countries—the rich and the poor alike ;the people of England and Scotland and Ireland and Wales. Of those countries Ireland is the poorest. Of those peoples the Irish are the most sorely oppressed by the weight of taxation. But I say that there is no Irishman so poor as to begrudge to.day his mite towards honouring the memory of this kindly, brave, and consistent friend of our country. Nothing that was said on Monday is a greater tribute to the ate Prime Minister.

..17-Sed-don, M.P. turd a good story at the meeting held in support of the Licensing Bill at Great Sankey on Monday evening. One morning a village cobbler was hard at work when the son of a neigh- bouring publican came rushing in excitedly with the request that he would go and help father to eject a drunken man. "No " was the cobbler's reply "When I have finished my jobs I put them in the window. Let your father do the same.'
