In the course of his speech at Liverpool on Wednes- day Mr. Joynson-Hicks said that although Noncon- formists might claim a monopoly of" conscience" and a monopoly of paying the rates, they could not claim to have all the children.—A man in the gallery : No. I've got nine. (Loud laughter,)—Mr. Joynson-Hicks : You have done your duty, sir. (Mote Laughter.) If there Were more like our friend there would be no single-school areas. (Loud laughter.) Lovers of music are reminded that the Warrington Musical Festival takes place at the Parr Hall to-day. No effort has been spared to present interesting and high-class programmes and we hope the promoters will be repaid by crowded audiences. Musical culture has made rapid strides in Warrington of late years and the town sliould certainly be able to bring to a successful issue an annual fcstival which is bound to do a great deal for the advancement of the divine art.

* * * It is stated in Liverpool that the advantages claimed for a direct service between Liverpool and New York are to be put to a practical test. The Cunard Com- pany will run the " Mauretania " across on an experimental trip without calling at Qaeenstown. The liner leaves the Mersey on Wednesday, the 27t11., and, given favourable conditions, may reach New York the following Monday night. It is expected that if this voyage comes up to expectations, arrangements will be made with the Government to drop Queenstown as a calling-point for the mail service.

div.head: EDUCATION NOTES.
div.p: EDUCATION NOTES.
BY I COIZIEESPONDEN7.

The most interesting part of the proceedings of the Education Committee on Monday night was Mr. Jolley's motion expressing dissatisfaction with the proposal of the Health Committee that the doctor responsible for the medical inspection of school children should reside at the infections diseases hospital. The motion gave rise to a very animated debate and finally was carried by sixteen votes to nine. The position taken up by the Health Corn- mittee is a truly amazing one. After all, the primary considerations .are not • the convenience of officials, and of. Committee', not even the proposed saving of £2OO a year (a doubtful saving at best), but the welfare of the children, and the wishes and feelings of the parents. It is all very well to say that it is all sentiment to object to a medical man coming from the Fever Hospital to examine children-__But sentiment prevents us eating snails (a nutritious diet) ; senti- ment makes us shrink from the embraces of a cockroach (a harmless insect), and sentiment plus common sense says that it is extremely undesirable that a doctor should come from an environment of infectious disease to examine school children, some of whom may be greatly susceptible to the disease, the germs of which he may carry upon his person or clothing.

The supply of teachers seems to have more than overtaken the demand. We understand that very few of the senior students in our local Training College i have secured places. This is the case n every Training College in the country and the prospects of immediate employment for many are rather gloomy. Under the circumstances we think it is time that the. employment of married women shall cease. There surely can be no reason for the continuance of married wotnen in the employment of Education Committees when a large number of single women dependent upon their own labour for their support are without occu- pation. The Warrington Committee has taken the right line from the first in refusing to employ married women except" on supp'y.", The Committee found a number of married women in the Schools and these have been retained although we have heard many murmurings as to their continued employment. The Lancashire and Cheshire Education Committees have been great sinners in the employment of married women, but the growing feeling against it will, we feel convinced,'compel all Education Authorities to dispense with their services. The sooner, the better.

From what Canon Stevenson said on Monday the question (if financial aid to the Grammar School has not yet been settled. It is difficult for an outsider to know what has been going on in Committee but we understand that the Governors ask as a condition for the acceptance of the new Regulations of the Board of Education a fixed grant from the rates in lien of the present arrangement by which their deficit is made good up to £4OO per annum. The question is a serious and important one. The Board of Education offers double grants to the Grammar School upon the under- standing that a majority_ of its Garernors_alm.lll6. representatives from publics bodies, that there shall, be no denominational teaching and that one-fourth of the places in the school shall be reserved for boys from the Elementary Schools. The members of the Town Council naturally expected that the governors would accept the new regulations thereby doubling their grants from Government and so relieve the Council from a large part of its contribution. We understand, however, that the governors ask for a definite sum annually from the Corporation irrespective of their income from endowments and grants. Whether they will get it remains to be seen.

The class teachers of Warrington are heartily to be commended upon their determination to make them- selves familiar with local industries. The Code and the " suggestions" governing the schools point out the desirability of teaching children more of the industries, geography and history of their immediate neighbourhood. The class teachers in pursuance of these aims have already visited a number of the works in the town and to-day they visit the establishment of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co. The thanks of all I —parents, teachers, children —are clue to those-manu- facturers who not only have thrown open their works to inspection but have taken pains to have the various processes f ally explained by expert officials and workmen.

The second reading of the Education Bill has been carried in the house of Commons by a majority of 164. There has been an approachment towards com- promise, and all educationists would heartily welcome a settlement. An aggressive attitude was taken by Mr. Balfour and several of his followers, which does not argue well for peace. We have no hesitation in saying that but for " contracting out " the Bill is a good one. It removes the just grievances of the Non- conformists, it deals fairly with the non-provided schools, and it is the charter of emancipation for the village teacher. But " contracting out ! ' Yet, what is the substitute? Nothing has yet been proposed which has not greater objections to it than " contract- ing out " has. The Prime Minister said that the objection to it seemed to rest not on the principle but on the amount of Government grant to be paid, and that might be a matter for negotiation. This would mean, of course, the administration of public funds by private individuals (the managers), and in any scheme of contracting-out a strict and searching annual Local Government Board audit should be insisted on of all the expenditure of the contracted out schools. The teachers should he paid on the same scale of salaries as those in the Municipd Schools and they should have reason- able security of tenure. These regulations would mitigate the evils of contracting out, but we must confess that we regard its adoption with some mis- giving. , In the interests alike of Religion and Education it is quite time the question was settled and we hope that during this Session the reasonable men of all parties will be able to arrive at some common basis of agreement.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S WATER
div.p: WARRINGTON'S WATER
SUPPLY.
OPPOSITION TO THE LIVERPOOL CORPORATION BILL.

The Police and Sanitary Regulations Committee d the House of Commons on Wednesday began the con sideration of that part of the Liverpool Corporation General Powers Bill which deals with questions of water supply. Mr. Leyland Barrett presided. The first subject dealt with was the proposal embodied in clause 16, that unless within three years from the Ist January last the Corporations of St. Helens, Warring- ton, and Widnes respectively demanded and agreed to take a supply of water from the Liverpool Corporation, the statutory agreements under which the Corporation bound itself to grant that supply should at the expira- tion of that period be cancelled. The counsel for the promoters were Mr. Balfour -Browne, K.C.,Mr. Lloyd, K.C.. and Mr. Gerald Fitz- gerald. Warrington was represented by Mr. Hutchinson St. Helens by Mr. Wedderburn, and Widnes by Mr. Raw K.C. and Mr. Jeeves. In his opening statement, Mr. Balfour Browne explained that in 1880 Liverpool came to Parliament for the great Vyrowy scheme. Warrington, Widnes and St. Helens petitioned against that bill. St. Helens urged that, as Liverpool had taken the Rivington area, which was in a sense their natural source of supply, they ought to be put under an obligation to supply St. Helens from Rivington. St. Helens at that time derived its supply from the red sandstone' and alleged that the water was unfit for domestio use. Widnes, which was also supplied from wells, said their wells were contaminated, that they had no adequate source of supply, and that their population was rapidly increasing, and they there- fore asked Parliament to require Liverpool to give them a supply from the Vyrnivy pipes. Warrington alleged that their aupply was deficient in quantity and in quality, and that Liverpool should be bound to supply them also from the Vyrnwy aqueduct. The Liverpool Corporation in 1880 had no objection to giving these places a supply by agreement, but they were unwilling to have a compulsory obligation put upon them. Parlianfent did not insist on a clause requiring Liver, pool to give a supply,but stipulated theta Parliamentary agreement should be entered into with Warrington. Widnes and St. Helens. It was assunted that the three towns werein immediate want of water,and would takes ,supply from Liverpool on the terms agreed upon almost at once. That was twenty-eight years ago, and up till now they had never taken a drop of water, and what Liverpool felt was that they were prevented from supply- ing other places with water by having these agreements hanging over their heads. Two yeass ago Birkenhead approached Liverpool for a supply. Liverpool negotiated I with Birkenhead, but when the matter came to be dis- cussed the City Council came to the conclusion that owing to the existence of these agreements, they could not grant the supply. and Birkenhead promoted its own bill. Liverpool Corporation had forty-nine different authorities dependent on them for water. If there was , a necessity, then the water would be supplied, and they had given each of the petitioners three years in which Ito make up their minds. But each of these towns, ' according to the view of Liverpool, had an ample supply of water, and there was no necessity for them to go to Liverpool. Why, then, should they be allowed to con- tinue to seal up in the Liverpool reservoirs a daily ' supply of six million gallons which they did not want? Alderman Burgess gave evidence bearing out counsel's statement.

Asked whether it was not as desirable now as it was in 1880 that Warrington should have as a stand-by this possible supply from Liverpool, Alderman purgess said that, if as was suggested, it was a very undesirable thing to go into the neighbourhood of colliery works for a water supply, it was a very unfortunate thing that War- rington should have gone there when it had the oppor- tunity all the time of going to Liverpooi and getting a supply there. The agreement provided for a minimum supply of 500,000 gallons a day, and a maximum of two million gallons, and the price for the smaller quantity was 6d. per 1,030 gallons, and for the larger quantity 51(1.

At what price, under like circumstances but apart from Parliamentary egret:neat, do you sell water out- side the compulsory limits P—We supply half a million gallons a day at 6d. per 1,000 gallons to Wallasey. Witness was not in a position to commit the Water Committee as to the price at which, if they had six million gallons to vend in quantities of half a million gallons, they would sell it. Would you not ask more than 6d ?—I am not going to commit the committee. Mr.J. Parry,chief water engineer, said the agreements, were one-sided because the Corporations were under no obligation to take water, and yet they might call upon Liverpool at any time to give it. It was a dog-in-the- manger policy of trying to hold on to an arrangement of which they never intended to take advantage. It operated prejudicially to third parties, as well as to the Corporation of Liverpool. By Mr. Hutchinson : Liverpool supplied the railway icompanies with water at 4d. per 1,003 gallons. This was in pursuance pf a Parliamentary bargain. There AT.§-nrm. The Alitne3s said, and there never had bean-, Any- question of selling water at a profit ; and that was not the ground on which the proposal was made. Mr. Raw (for Widnes) suggested that as the water supply of Widnes was more precarious now than in 1890, it was more likely now than it was then that Widnes would shortly want a supply from Liverpool. Witness replied that the• uncertainty had now con- tinued for twenty-eight years, and the time had arrived, when it should be terminated. Liverpool asked for a time-limit, because the understanding when the agree- ment was made was that Widnes would require and would take a supply as soon as the Vyrnwy works were completed. Widnes would have no more claim upon Liverpool than anybody else ?—Liverpool had never yet refused to grant a supply to any authority along the lines of the aqueduct on terms that are extremely fair and reason- able.

Mr. G. F. Deacon, water engineer, examined by Mr. Fitz Gerald, said he was clearly of opinion, in view, of the hardship which the agreements imposed upon it, the Corporation ought to be required to exercise their options within a reasonable time. The Committee adjourned. The committee again sat on Thursday, when Mr. G. F. Deacon continued his evidence.

By Mr. Hutchinson (for Warrington) : Ile thought the agreements were imposed upon Liverpool upon evidence which was entirely misleading. If Warrington in 1880 grounded its claim to a right of supply on its vested right to the use of the Mersey, under which the aqueduct was carried, then he would point out that in the Act of 1880 Liverpool granted a clause safeguarding that vested right which satisfied Warrington, the details being left to be settled by the Board of Trade. He admitted that at present Liverpool had 121 million gallons of water running to waste at Vyrncvy. Mr. Hutchinson, in putting the case for the Corpora- tion of Warrington, said tho courso which the Com- mittee was asked by Liverpool to take involved the destruction of a broad Parliamentary principle—the conservation of national resources. Parliament said "In order to conserve what we regard as a natural supply of water and to the safeguard necessities which might arise, but which might not be foreseen now, we will put upon you the obligation that if and when that necessity does arise you shall, !Tan demand, satisfy it." It had been suggested that this agreement was a con- cession granted out of Liverpool's generosity. It was nothing of the kind. The words of the chairman of the committee of 1880 were, "we have required and secured, &c." This was not an application to relieve Liverpool from any onerous agreement that it had voluntarily and incautiously entered into, but a deliberate attempt to upset long-established Parliamentary usage,and to take away legislative advan- tages given to other communities. There was another Parliamentary principle—viz., that where conveniences were afforded by a community Parliament had in some instances imposed an obligation to supply. The whole of Warrington's petition in 1880 was in respect of the facilities then to be granted to Liverpool, and no ques- tion was then raised as to the recessity of a supply for Warrington being imminent. Liverpool had water to last her for many years, and on physical grounds, and apart from the agreement, the case absolutely dis- appeared. The committee adjourned till Tuesday morning.

div.head: EMPIRE DAY.
div.p: EMPIRE DAY.
Territorials' Church Parade.

To-morrow (Sunday) is Empire Day, and it is expected that allusions to the occasion mill be made at the various places of worship. In the morning the members of the 4th Battalion (P.W.V.) South Lanca- shire Regiment will attend service at the Parish Church. They will assemble at 9.45 in service dress, and only those who have joined the territorial force will be allowed to take part in the parade. At Wycliffe Church in the evening the Rev. John ,Yonge will preach on 1" Empire Day : It's Use and Misuse." I The Empire Day celebrations at the elementary schools will take place on Monday, when the Mayor and Mayoress, following out their programme of twelve months ago, will visit 20 schools, accompanied by the Chairman of the Education Committee (Councillor Fulton-Smith) and other gentlemen. A time-table has been drawn up, and almost every minute of the day will be occupied. The first school to be visited is St. Ann's, where the party will arrive at 9.10. The last visit, at 4.10, will be to the Secondary School. No visit to a school is to occupy more than five minutes, except perhaps, in the Secondary School. The Mayor and Mayoress will present medals and brooches to those boys and girls who, by the vote of their fellow scholars, have been adjudged the best scholars in the school. His Worship will also present an autograph portrait of himsel,4

The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Tuesday of Mr. John Looker, licensee of the Hop Pole Hotel, Horsemarket-street, who was well known and esteemed in the town. He had been ailing for a considerable time and passed away at the age of 53, on Friday, the cause of death being pleurisy. He leaves a widow, three sons and three daughters. Mr. Looker had been the licensee of the Hop Pole Hotel for nearly four years. Prior to that he was an engine driver in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company for 29 years. He was closely identified with St. Barnabas' Church and filled the office of churchwarden for about twelve years. The funeral was conducted by the Rev. -J. H. G. Hollingworth, vicar of St. Barnabas Church. The chief mourners were : Mrs. Looker (widow), Misses Gertrude, Sarah and Harriet Looker (daughters), Messrs John, William sod Joseph Looker (sons). The following engine-drivers acted as bearers : —Messrs. T. Plinston, J. Pennington, W. Siddall, T. Silcock, W. Taylor, and J. Shaw. The licensed victuallers were represented by : —Messrs. T. Walsh, G. Davies (Penketh), Peers Brimelow, Thompson, J. McLinton, Joseph Hatton. Amongst others present were Mr. and Mrs. Broadhurst (brother and sister-in-law), Mrs. Eaves (sister); Mrs. Benjamin Looker (cousin), Mrs. William Looker (cousin), Airs. Looker (daughter-in-law),llfra.Joseph Looker (daughter- in-law), qrs. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

WIDNES BURNING FATALITY. Emily Garner, twenty-three years of age, of Cholmondeley-street, Widnes, was admitted to the Widnes Accident Hospital a week ago suffering from severe burns on the legs and body. She had been employed as servant at South-lane -Farm, Bold, and, whilst putting a pan of water upon the fire, her clothing was seen to blaze. The " flames were quickly extinguished, aul she was brought to the Widnes Hospital in the horse ambalance. Her condition from the first MIS critical, and she lingered until Sunday evening, when she died at 8.15. RAID ON A FARYIYARD.

At Widnes, on Monday, John Devereux, a burly Newtown youth, was charged with being on the enclosed premises of Mr. Sparkes, of Denton Farm, near Widnes, on Saturday night. From the evidence it transpired that the complainant heard his dog bark about twelve o'clock, and on going outside he saw three men. He asked them what they were doing and they ran away. Prisoner fell down, and Sparkes, giving chase, nearly fell over him, and both struggled on the grouna. Prisoner got away, but Mr. Sparkes followed him, and the struggle was resumed in Frank-street. Sparkes said he kept hens, clucks, and pigeons, and he suspected that the men were about to raid his place.— Police-constable Hill said he went to the prisoner's home in Wahusley-street and overheard a conversation from the window. Prisoner had left his clothes behind and by these he was identided.—Devereus said he was mad drunk at the time and knew nothing about it. In answer to the charge he only replied, " Loud applause amongst the shillings."—The bench committed him to gaol for two months for being on enclosed premises, and on a further charge for assaulting Sparkes, he was sent to gaol for two months hard labour.

div.head: ATTE It PTE D SIJICIDE.
div.p: ATTE It PTE D SIJICIDE.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. E. Imison and John Littler, John Price, a middle-aged man, was charged on remand with having attempted to commit suicide by drowning in a pit at Rock Savage on Saturday week.—The Magistrates' Clerk, having informed the magistrates that prisoner had been in gaol for a week, asked him whether he was all right now.—Prisoner : Yes, sir.—You had been drinking for two or three days before you attempted to drown yourself ?—Yes.—ls there any fear that you will repeat the attempt ?—No. You are going to live with your sister ?—Yes. The Chairman said there was a probability that prisoner would be able to get work and a home. He would be bound over to keep the peace for six cuonths.—Prisoner : I wish to thank Superintendent Ennion's son for having rescued me.—The Chairman : Quite right. You were very fortunate to be saved. There is no doubt you owe your life to Mr. Ennion's bravery. It must be a satis- faction to him and to the Superintendent that he was instrumental in saving a Mo.—Superintendent Conlon: Thank you, sir. lam proud to know I have a son able to do it. It was more than I could have done. I could manage what was done on the bank, but I couldn't where it was wet. (Laughter).—The Chairman : The attention of the Royal Humane Society ought to be drawn to the case.

div.head: ST. lIELEN S.
div.p: ST. lIELEN S.
WIFE'S TERRIBLE STRUGGLE.

Thomas Francis Hallvvood, of Wood-street, wa charged at St Helens on Saturday with having attempted to commit suicide. The evidence was that on Friday the man, who had had some drink, went home from the fair, afterwards going to a drawer where hi a razor was, telling his wife that he was going to cut his throat,and that he would not be in her way long. She struggled with him, and dragged the razor from him, and after smashing the handle with the poker, threw the blade down a grid in the street. Police-constable Adams afterwards came on the scene. 4lallwood than became very excited, and repeatedly said he was determined to cut his throat. Mrs. Hallwood, in her evidence, said her husband was a good man, and only did this kind of thing when he was in drink. The magistrates remanded the man for a week.
ST. HELEN'S COLLIER'S SUICIDE.
DECAPITATED BY A TRAIN.

Early on Tuesday morning the body of -a man with his head cut off was found on the railway near Thatto Heath Station, St. Helens. From the position of tie body it appeared to be a case of suicide, the man having placed his neck on the rail and allowed the train to pass over him.—lt was found that the body was that of Henry Martindale, aged twenty-eight, a collier, of 214. Nutgrove-road.—Martindale's father had been looking for him until late in the night, as he was afraid that deceased, who had been ont of work for some weeks, was "on the spree." The tragic act appears to have taken place about 2 a.m., when a goods train from Black- burn to Liverpool was passing through the rock cutting at Thattp Hoath. A COLLIER'S CONIPENSATION.

_ At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, a dispute under the Workmen's Compensation Act came before his Honour Julge Shoed, between Joseph Rylance, collier, of Houghton-street, Prescot, and Latham Bros., the proprietors of Eccleston Hall Colliery Company. Mr. Stewart Brown, instructed by Mr. W. Ilutchen appeared for Rylance, and said that on May 27 last year Rylance, when working in the Eccleston Hall Colliery, was knocked down and crushed by a fall of roof, when the muscles of his back were sprained and the spinal column injured. He was totally incapacitated, and was paid 15s. 9d. per week up to November 12, when he resumed work. He worked in the mine until January 14 this year, a period of eight weeks, but did so under great clatriculty, and had to give up work. Since that 1 time the respondents had refused to pay compensation. The man hod not been offered light work, but all that he was told was that he had fully recovered. Mr. Cnthbert Smith (instructed by Forwood and Williams), said his view was that the company might find some employment which would suit Rylance. The Judge allowed the case to stand over in order that some arrangement could be come to. The judge, by consent, made an award for £l5 arrears of compensation. with 10s. in future on respondents, in addition finding Rylance work in the lamp-room with a, minimum wage of 15s, a week. NEW ST. HELENS LABOUR CLUB. ADDRESS BY MR. GLOVER, M.P. Mr. Thomas Glover, M.P. on Saturday night attended the formal opening of the East Sutton Labour Club. St. Helens Junction, where commodious premises have been secured.—Mr. Charles Walsh presided over a large gathering.—Mr. Glover wished the club every success, and said he had no doubt it would be conducted in a straight and manly way In a reference to current politics he said he supported the second reading of the Licensing Bill because he did not believe that it was a bill of confisca- tion and robbery, as they were told by the, brewers. He hoped the Govern,nent would deal with the clubs. There were bona-fide working men's clubs all over the country which were doing a large amount of good in lifting up the people, but there were also a large number of clubs which ought to be closed which were nothing else but tied houses to breweries. He knew clubs where brewers had found the money to build the club so that they could supply it with drink, and he ktievv of clubs that had been struck off the register because of the drinking and gambling which had been going on. They did not want clubs which were simply drinking clubs, because they did incalculable harm to the working-man. He did not think it ought to be possible for a man to go out of a public-house at eleven o'clock, walk across the road into a club, and stop there drinking two or three hours longer, but he thought the club should be closed at the same time as public-houses. He was very anxious that the time-limit should be insisted upon, and rather than have that part of the Bill given up he would be in favour of the time being extended. He would also like to see an Education Bill brought for- ward which would meet the requirements of everybody. It was a right, principle that the parents should have the right to hrive their children taught the religion they desired. He believed that when the Education Bill again came up there would be a meeting of the various bodies for the purpose of trying to arrange a measure which would be satisfactory to all concerned.

Professional Foot Races. A crowd of 4,000 assembled on the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday afternoon, the attraction being an athletic meeting promoted by Alfred Shrubb, the world's champion long distance runner. The chief event was the attack made by Shrubb on his own grass track record for four miles of 19min. 20 4-ssec. G. B. Tinder, of Edinburgh was announced as his opponent, to whom he was to have conceded 100 yards start. For some unexplained reason, however,Tincler, although on the ground in the early part of the after- noon, failed to turn out, and Shrubb made his effort paced by three runners of smile repute. He gave an exhibition of wonderful staying powers, covering the 23 laps in 20min. 20 4-ssec., which is a capital performance considering that the turf was rather heavy after the recent rains. Another important event was the 120 yards race between W. Growcott, of Banbury, Cheshire,and B. R. Day, of Blackpool, the latter receiving a yard start. For the 100 yards open handicap for professional footballers only eight competitors out of 17 entries turned out. J. Fish, Warrington, (five yards start) was beaten by A. Cawdery, Broughton Rangers (12) in the first heat. In the final E. 13racegirdle, Black- burn Rovers (91) NVOII by four yards, R. Spicer, Leigh (8) being second, half a yard in front of A. Cawdery (12). Time lOsec. It. Spicer, the champion jumper of the world, gave an exhibition of trick jumping over chairs but failed to jump over a cart- horse 18 hands high. He then made an attempt to beat J. Higgins 's world's record for four hops and a jump of 57ft. Pin, and he was successful by nine inches. The officials were : —Judges, Messrs. H. Ashton, W. Price and F. Turner ; starter, Mr. A. Bailey ; and stewards, Messrs. W. Price, B.Parsonage, Anderton, A. Gleave, R. Anderton and S. Parson- age. During the afternoon Crosflelds Band played choice selections.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

A RHEUMATIC PONY. Last Thursday at Newton Petty Sessions Isaac Taylor, of Legh-street, Earlestown, pleaded not guilty to a charge of cruelty to a pony in Vista-road on April 22nd.—Inspector 'lye, of the E.S.P.C.A. said he stopped the defendant's son, who was with the horse and a firewood cart. The horse was lame in both fore- legs and in poor condition. The load was not a heavy one and he did not wish to press it as a bad case.— Delendant, who said it was rheumatism, and the horse was not lame except when it caught cold, was let otion payment of costs. UNUSUAL THEFT CASE.

- - - At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, William , Picton was charged with stealing two oak-framed chairs the property of 'homes Lythgoe, worth £2, on May 4. —lhomas Fairclougn deposed that he bought, for .11r. Phonies Lythgoe, licensed victualler, a dining-room suite at the sale of the late Dr. Patterson's furniture in Cross Lane, Earlestown, but when he wanted to take the chairs away these two were missing.—Patrick j Urorman, of Broad Oak Road, St. Helens, doposed that ;he was at the sale and the prisoner gave him Is. Gd. to I help him to remove the cuairs. lie afterwards told witness he was to say he knew nothing about it.— William broker, of High-street, Newton, said the prisoner told him he had bought the chairs at 83. each, and he left them with witness. P.C. Lennie said that he was at Dr. Patterson's sale, off duty, and saw the prisoner there. On information subsequently received ne apprehended the prisoner, who admitted the offence, and said it was done at every sale. —Mr. Longton, for the defence, said the defendant was a respectable joiner, of H.aydock, and the only reason he could give for the offence wa% that being out of work and distressed, he took the chairs in a moment Of temporary aberration. He (Mr. Longton) had a letter from Dr. Dowling expressing that opinion. Defendant's father and orother were in Court, and willing to be bound for Ills good behaviour if that would satisfy the Bench.—The Bench agreed to this, and prijoner was liberated on the recognizances of himself` his father and brother.

MR. VICTOR GRAYSON, M.P., AT EARLES TOWN* A demonstration in connection with the Earlestown Socialists was held on Saturday night at the Town Hall, Earlestown. Mr. Victor Grayson, M.P., was the principal speaker. The chair was taken by Mr. Didsbnry. Mr. Grayson said every child was born into a state of society known by the phrase " white slavery." The fact they should burn into their hearts was that under the existing system a human being who was employed as a labourer was not counted as a human soul at all. The soul was an inconvenient illusion. When he used to attend his economic classes the learned professor used to call the working classes so many • human cubic feet of labour power." It was no use to talk about equal education and the chew.° of every child to rise to be, say, the head of the Local Government Board. They were born shackled and handicapped, and it was no use shirking an obvious fact. It was the number of women in the Colne Valley that won the election for him. Wherever the !women joined their movement it proved a " howling " ' success, and he explained that he meant the word howling " literally. (Laughter and applause.) Referring to the Licensing Bill, Mr. Grayson said that it was not the brewers that made drunkards. The very men who were prating in the House of Commons— chiefly employers of labcur—about the sins of the brewers were responsible for the country's drunkenness. The things he had seen in this country kept him recon- secreted to Socialism. Whenever a capitalist hireling told him to defend his country he wanted to ask that. man to show him his country and he would defend it. The people had no access to the land, which was staked out by a small number of haman beings. The following resolution was carried : That this meeting of Earles- town and distriot Socialists heartily adirms its unswerv- ing belief in Socialism as the only cure for present-day industrial troubles." HAY DOCK FANMERS' LITIGATION. ANOTHER JURY DISAGREEMENT. Mr. Justice Pickford and a common jury, at Liver- pool Assizes, on Monday, continued the hearing of the action "Berry v. Wright," commenced on Thursday. At the March Assizes Mr. Justice Ridley and a jury spent nearly twil days in trying the case, but the jury disagreed. The original form ot the action was a claim by John Berry, Florida Farm, Ilaydock, for £I2G balance of the price of two stacks of hay, but that sum was afterwards paid, and the case now came before the court upon the entry of the defendaut,Peter Wright, a farmer and hay and straw dealer, of Rainhill, who sought to recover damages in respect of allaged breach of warranty of the hay. Wright's case was that on November 1 last year he bought two stacks of what he understood to be clover hay from Berry, at the agreed price of £230. The stacks were, he contended, warranted to be -of the best quality, free from rakings, and got in during a good week. The hay, however, he found was not what he expected. He had paid £4 in cash and a cheque for £lOO, and on January 2 handed Berry a cheque for £126, balance of the price. When be found that the hay was not the quality expected he stopped payment of the cheque for £126. The counterclaim was for ZTh, the difference between what Wright said he got for the hay when he sold it and what he should have gut it the hay had been what he expected. Berry's contention was that the hay was good clover hay, and free from takings or rubbish. He further denied that he gave a warranty, and said that Wright bought the hay after examining it himself. Mr. Taylor, K.C., Mr. Rigby Swift, and Mr. Bodell (instructed by Mr. Arthur Smith, of Wigan) were counsel for Berry; and Mr. Langdon, K.C., and Mr. Layton (instructed by Mr. R. Barrow-Sicree) represented Wright. When the hearing was resumed on Monday additional evidence was adduced to support Berry's view of the matter.

Counsel on each side addressed the jury, and the Judge summed up. The jury, after an absence from court of close upon two hours, intimated that there was !whop° of a verdict being agreed upon. His Lordship consequently discharged them. MR. SEDDON, M.P., AND TEIE COAL CONSU SIERS' LEAGUE.

Mr. J. A. Sal-d-013,-Ik-In.-VTior-KOWt-on -Division, was present on Saturday night at the inauguration of a new Labour Club at the East-end of Ilaydock. Mr. W. Speakman (chairman of the Newton Labour party) pre- sided.—Mr. Seddon spoke in terms of approval of what the divisional Labour party had done during the past few years in the constituency, and said that the club was welcome as another centre of activity. They ' all looked forward to the Government treating the club question fairly and equitably in the Licensing Bill, and so far as the Labour party was ' concerned they had nothing to fear from the inspection clauses of the bill. Referring to the outcry against the Licensing Bill, Mr. Seddon said that the men who were opposing it were the same men who had been opposing everything that had!been demanded by the workers of the country. In that, as well as in the question of the Miner's Eight Hours Bill, they saw how capital was against labour. For twenty years the miners' representatives had been lobbying members and trying to push it forward. Immediately the Labour party entered Parliament they brought in the Bill, and then, lo and behold, the Coal Consumers' League sprung into being. Who were the coal consumers ? Were they the people who actually used the coal, or were they the representatives of capital ? The Coal Consumers' League consisted of men like Lord Newton, who had great interost in mining royalties, and took 6d. for every ton of coal which they raised. That was the kind of opposition which the Coal Consinners' League repre- sented. He denied that the Eight Hours Bill would increase the price of coal, £1 nd said that if the mines were fitted out with good travelling roads and a plentiful supply of " boxes," or waggons, the men wculd raise quite as much coal in the eight hours as they did at present. With regard to old-age pensions, he welcomed the Government's scheme as a beginning, but said that the Labour party would not be satisfied until they got at least is. (id. for every man and woman who reached the age of sixty-five. The rich people had looked after themselves in the past,and it was time that the workers paid some attention to their own needs. _

div.head: IT OPENS TO-DAY.
div.p: IT OPENS TO-DAY.
THE NEW BRIGHTON TOWER AND PARR' WITH 100 ATTRACTIONS.

Preliminary to the opening of New Brighton Tower and Park to-day, the management yesterday, Friday, made a most picturesque parade of their various attractions through the principal streets of Liverpool, and the Wirral Peninsular. The parade started from the Lime-street Station at 10 o'clock, and proceeded around St. George's Hall, and passed through Elliott, Church, Lord, Castle and Water-streets to the Pierhead, where embarkation was made for the Tower. The formal opening of the Tower and Parks takes place at 10 o'clock this, Saturday morning, and from a visit made on Thursday, it can readily be seen that to all intents and purposes this popular place of resort has been made for and is a new recreation ground in its entirety, for with the exception of the Tower Theatre and Ballroom and a few of the smaller but more popular attractions of the past, the ground is practically covered with new structures, new shows, and new devices for the enter- tainment and recreation of visitors to New Brighton. It is the purpose of the new management to so improve this park that it shall be, not only in the number and variety as well as the novelty of its attractions—the most complete park in England, but in its conduct,shall be the safest resort for the entertainment of ladies and rchildren and all others who may desire a clean, whole- some place for spending a pleasant day.

The almost incomprehensible action of the Town Council and the discreditable conduct of the Chairman of the Health Committee justified, he thought, the course he was about to take. Mr. JOLLEY then submitted a long history of the negotiations between the Health Committee and the Education Authority. Dealing with the Health Com- mittee's latest proposal, that the duties of medical inspection of school children should be peformed by a medical officer resident at the Aiken-street Hospital, he said the Aiken-street Hospital was an infectious diseases hospiSal, and the proposal that the resident Medical Officer should go out and perform work laid down by the new Act in the schools of the town—well, it was difficult to characterize without using un-Parliamentary language. He did not want to say anything unnecessarily "offensive, though some very astonishingly offensive things had been said about the Education Committee on more than one occasion by one or two members of the Town Council, and one would be perfectly justified in using some strong language in connection with this. He said without hesitation that the action of the Health Committee came little short of criminal folly. The proposal was in his judgment an iniquitous one, and he asked that committee to mark their sense of the way in which the subject had been treated by adopting his proposal, if not unanimously,by a big majority. He asked them to do it in the public interests. He denounced the suggestion of the Health Committee; he denounced it in the name of the ratepayers. They had been told this was going to be a cheap scheme. It was nasty, but it was not really cheap. The financial interests of the ratepayers would suffer by the pro- posal of the Health Committee. He denounced it in the interests of the parents whose feelings would be outraged, and be denounced it in the name of the children whose lives would be imperilled.. If the resolution of the Health Committee was carried into effect, and a medical officer was appointed who spent his leisure and rest time in the centre of infection, there would bo created a consider- able difficulty with the parents of a considerable numter of the children in regard to the inspection. Joseph proposed as a public man fur the welfare or te children must be right. It would be hard to estimate the damage which had ,been done by the expressions of opinion which had been given that evening. The medical officer might be at the hospital a month before he had an emergency c.so, and if a gentleman could not live within the conliaes of the building, but not in the wards' all the houses in the neighbourhood should be closed. When there was an outbreak of infection the schools were closed and that showed that the Health Committee were cautious and would do the best they could. (A Voice: "Question.") The Health Committee if anything, were over careful. The Medical Officer was to be within call, not in the wards. He was to be there to save the life of a child who might be choking during the night, and he did not run the risk the ordinary practitioner ran in Warrington. Mr. KINODON asked whether it was not a fact that the majority of educational authorities in the country had appointed their own assistant medical officer to deal with this particular Act under their own juris- diction and control. If this meeting approved of Mr. Jolley's motion, and the Health Committee refused to alter the arrangement, what would he their position? Councillor WatetelsoN advised Mr. Jolley when he commenced an argument not to do so in the warm way in which he had Introduced his motion that evening. He objected to him speaking as he had done about the Chairman of the Health Committee, especially in his absence, as he regarded it as hitting below the belt. They had a respected chairman in Councillor -Jatees Evans, Indeed Warrington had never had a harder working man. Mr. Jolley should have told the meet- ing that the memorandum of the Board of Education said distinctly that the Local Education Authority— and that was the Town Council—were advised that they could utilize their existing machinery in carrying out the Act. The mattAr was only in the experi- mental stage at present. What had been said that night would have one object and that would be to set the town on Are. (Mr. Jolley : You are quite right.) Richardson. 1 Mr. Jeans (the local hon. secretary( reports as follow 's : - The Warrnigton and District branch of the National Saciety for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children has during the qnarter ended 31st March inquired into 81 complaints of neglect, ill-treatment and other wrongs of childhood, of which all were found to be true, affecting 275 children and 128 offenders. Action was taken as follows: 72 cases were warned, 9 were prosecuted (convicted 9). The society's inspector made 379 visits of supervision. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER TIM CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Adyt. Unhappy Married Life. At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday,Sarah Ellen Kendall was granted a separation order, with a weekly allowance of 6s. from her husband, Edward Kendall, on the ground of his being an habitual drunkard. It was stated by Mr. Steel, for the com- plainant, that the parties had been married eight years, and during that time the • husband had been addicted to excessive drinking. He had lost two situations through his intemperate habits. His wife had several times forgiven him, but his conduct was now unbearable. Ex-Governor's Son Sentenced. At Frodsham, on Wednesday, Kirkwood Wilson Braid, described as a clever, educated workman, son of an ex-prison governor,was sentenced to three months' hard labour for neglecting his three young children. It was stated defendant was continually drinking while his wife and children starved at home. Since the sumnrms was issued one child had died of scarlet fever, and the other children had been fed by neighbours. Premier in name, Premier in quality. PREMIER CYCLES from 6 glimeas.-1. GARLAND, 51 to 55 Bridge-street,Warrington.— drt. Not Missed. Alfred Davies, a stranger, pleaded guilty at the Werrington Police Court, on Thursday morning to stealing a lady's jacket, value 153., from the dwelling- house of May Jane Wright, Rose and Crown street. Prisoner attempted to pledge the jacket at a local pawnshop, but the pawnbroker, being suspicions, informed the police, who made inquiries, and found that the article had been stolen. The prosecutor had not missed the jacket until informed by the police. The magistrates sent the prisoner to gaol for three months. Theft by a " Boots." George Thompson, 17 years of age,' " boots" at the Lion Hotel, Warrington,pleaded guilty at the Borough I Court, on Wednesday, to a charge of stealing a bicycle, the property- of Mr, John Lee. Superintendent Monaghan stated that in August last the prisoner was employed as a page-boy at the Lion Hotel, but he was discharged. He was subsequently re-engaged as " boots" until Friday last,when he disappeared,taking the bicycle with him. Prisoner was arrested at Birkenhead on Tuesday, and it was ascertained that he had exchanged the bicycle for a watch and a sum of money.—Prisoner was bound over in the sum of £lO under the Probation of Offennders Act. Lancashire Education Committee. Lancashire Education Committee met at Preston on Monday, when it was stated, in reply to a question as to the position of secondary schools in the county, that the apparent deadlock was owing to the inactivity of the Local Gr -at Board and the Law Office-- of

- encouraging the men to look after and keep clean the working horses of the town. The improvement in the condition of the horses during the past few years had been very marked. No matter how poor a horse a man had, or how poor a vehicle and harness, he should do his best with what he had, because the judges had , had the definite instructions that it was ' the men who had the worst things to work upon to whom the most credit was due: I It was forty minutes after the advertised time when the parade left the ground to traverse the principal streets, which were thronged with spectators. While there were no very original or picturesque features, the sight of so many well-kept and gaily-caparisoned Ihorses was impressive and there was a consensus of opinion that the parade did credit to all concerned. As usual Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. and Peter Walker and Son made a fine display with their powerful draught horses and other firms who were particularly well to the fore were the Warrington Slate Co.,Limited, who carried off some of the chief championship awards, and the Warrington Co-operative Society. The Corporation had also some splendid horses in ' the procession. A special word of praise should be I accorded to Mr. Peter Cartwright (entered as a work- ing horse owner), who gained the first prize against coal merchants and dealers, his being the class of entry the committee are anxious to encourage, and of which a special feature has been made this year. There were one or two rather novel displays. The one which attracted most attention was a capital repre- sentation on a luny of the " Children of Warrington INo. 1 Cot" at the Infirmary. The " patient " was , little Mis 3 Ethel Roberts, a relative of the late Alder- man John Roberts, and it was fitting that she should have been selected as the late Alderman for a con- siderable number of years manifested the greatest interest in the Infirmary and occupied the office of chairman of the Infirmary Working stifen's Cora- -1 mittee from its inception 'until his death. A large model of the Mayflower yacht, sent by the Seamen's Mission, Runcorn, added another touch of variety. In it were seated several ambulance m7n, amongst others being Captain Waring, the chief superintendent of the local St. John Ambulance Corps. In another smart conveyance were several daintily ; dressed young ladies playing mandclines. There were two bands in the procession—Walker's Brewery and the Borough,and their selections considerably enlivened the proceedings. The three local fire brikades Corporation, Wilderspool,and Crosfield's—madesmArt turnouts with their brightly burnished helmets and prettily decorated engines. Superintendent Frank Turner was in charge of the Warrington men, Captain Joseph Craughton in charge of the Wilderspool con- tingent and Second Officer Flood (in the absence of Captain Layton) in charge of Crosfield's Fire Brigade, The large crowds which lined the route had plenty of opportunities of contributing to the Infirmary and District Nursing Association' a small army of youthful collectors, with red cross badges, being in attendance and reaping a good harvest of coins. Mr. William Cooke, F.R.C.0., of Runcorn, has been appointed organist and choirmaster at Lymm Parish Church. Since 1900 Mr. Cooke has been organist and choirmaster at All Saints' Church, Sutton, St. Helens, his first appointment being at St. Paul's Church, Widnes, in 1816.

A painter, when just beginning to make a name in the artistic world, lived and executed many of his pictures in a small villa in a suburb 'of London. One day, as the one and only maid (a girl of sixteen) was cleaning the front-door steps, a man came along hawking cheap and gaudy pictures. "Good morning, miss," said he. No answer. "I say, my clear." Still no answer. "Look 'ere. is yer master hill? Don't yer think 'e could do with a couple o' cheap uns? Go in sn' anst 'im—there's a nice gal." Then the "nice gal" conthscended to look round, and with a disdainful sniff, snapped out: "Garn away! We makes 'em ourselves!"

With the saddening example of the unem- ployed as a text, the school teacher was en- deavouring to impress the idea of the wrong and danger of idleness upon her charges. "Now, children," she said, "I want to find out how much attention you've been paying. Tell me who is the miserable person who gets clothes and food and lodging, and yet does nothing in return?", There was dense silence in tha class, and, even after the lapse of twenty seconds, only one hand went up in response. Nellie," said the instructor, "who is it?" "Please, miss, the baby !" said Nellie.

"Oh, are yer?" came from the hero's friend. " Then if you'll tell Nelson 'is kitchen chimley's afire and 'is wife's jest 'ad a couple o' fits, p'raps 'e won't die so blessed lingerin'."

"This way for the heduc.ated 'oss," shouted a cockney showman as the writer pressed for- ward to catch a glimpse of Alpha, the intel- lectual equine who is presently showing him- self off at the Royal Aquarium. The mental feats he accomplishes are wonderful. Being asked to do a sum in addition, he irdicated the figures by taps with his fore-foot, one tap for one, two for two, and so on. He never makes a mistake. Subtraction to him id perfectly easy, and he subtracts one long row of figures from anoth3r by the "tapping" method with the ac- curacy of a good arithmetician. At nap he is an adept, and invariably wine any game of cards he chooses to play. Alpha adds music to his other accomplish- ments. A piano has been specially made for his use, and he is proficient in several simple tunes. His favourite piece is "God Save the King," and this he plays with his fore-feet, in a manner quite recognisable to musical ears. In his leisure hours he practises anthems and other high-class musical productions. Alpha claims to be the greatest player in the world. The method of training is simplicity itself, and horses can easily be trained to perform a variety of tricks by following these rules. Win the horse's affection. Feed him with your own hand, and never treat him unkindly. Little by little teach him some simple trick, such as lying down at the word of command, or bending down on his right or left knee Soon he will become proficient in easy accomplishments, and take a pleasure in them. Too many masters spoil the intellectual horse. He should have one tamer, and no other person should be al- lowed to interfere with him in any way.

"flow stupid you look always Slaring up into the sky," said, the buttercup to the daisies. "What can you see there?" "See? Oh, we see the bright sun, the blue sky, the soft summer clouds, and more wonders and beauties than we can tell," said the daisies. "But your necks ate quite stiff by it, and all the flowers laugh at you," said the buttercup. "We do not mind that in the least," replied the daisies. "What poor looking things the bluebdlls are! Don't you think so?" asked the buttercup. "Are they?" said the daisies. "As for that gaudy poppy, well, it is bold, standing so tall and holding its head so high. I should be ashamed to be like it." "Friend," said the daisies, "we may seem stupid to be always staring at the sky; but if you did the same you would avoid much that disturbs your mind and spoils your temper." ALICE IRONS.

THE TWO TWO SENTINELS. A cobbler sat at his bench. He was putting iron plates on the toes of some old boots to make them last a bit longer. By the fireside there was a basket partly covered with a cloth, and just by the basket a kitchen chair. Two cats sat side by side, just like two sentinels keeping guard. So closely did they watch the basket that,they neither moved nor turned their eyes. A visitor called. "What are the cats doing?" he asked. "Oh, they're watching the chickens. The chickens are just hatched." The basket was full of chickens. "Really? And won't they kill them?" "No, they won't. They killed a. sparrow among the chickens in the yard this morning, and won't let any one take the sparrow away from them; but they take care of the chickens." "That's very strange. Did you train them?" The cobbler told the visitor that when the cats were kittens they learned they must not hurt the chickens, and now they were as good as fathers to them.
"Well, to be sure," said the visitor, as pretty a sight as I ever saw." ETHEL SCHOFIELD. THE MAN IN THE MOON.

. -+--- A CHINAMAN'S DOGS.

Once upon a time there was a Chinaman who owned three dogs. He also had a eouch which he greatly valued. One evening he came home and found the dogs sleeping on this beautiful couch. He upset,and whipped them. The next night he came home the dogs were dutifully lying on the floor, but when he touched the couch he found it was still warm from the heat of their bodies. So he whipped them again. The next night coming home a little earlier than usual he found the dogs sitting in front of the couch blowing on it to make it cool. LILY WATSON.
THE GOOSE THAT LAID THE GOLDEN EGGS.

Once upon a time there was a man who had a goose he thought a great deal of. And well hp might do so, for this was the strangest goose that ever lived. Every day she laid an egg which was of solid gold, You may be sure he did not take these eggs to market and sell them, but hid them safely in an iron box. When he went to bed at night he could not sleep for thinking about the egg he hoped to find in the morning. He would rub his hands with glee, and say to himself, "If the box was only full I should ba the richest man in the world." He could think of nothing else, and soon he became so greedy that he wanted his box full without waiting. He thought the goose's body must be full of eggs, and so he killed her to get them all at once. But when he came to look for more eggs there were none to be found. Silly man! in his haste fr. ha ri eh hp had killed the goose that laid the golden eggs. GrAns's KILBr.

div.head: 4- A MISCHIEVOUS MONKEY.
div.p: 4- A MISCHIEVOUS MONKEY.

On board the ship in which I was coming to England we had a mischievous monkey called Jack. One day the men had been painting the ship outside, and were putting a broad band of white upon her. They went to dinner below, leaving their paint and brushes on the upper deck. Jack made signs to a little black monkey, who meekly obeyed the summons. Seizing his victim with one hand and foot, he took the brush with the other and covered the little black Monkey with the, white paint from head to foot. The laugh of the man at the helm called my attention to what was going on. As soon as Jack saw that he was discovered he dropped his painted brother and tan off up the rigging till he gained the top of the mast, where he stood looking 'at what was going on down below. As the other monkey began to lick him- self I called up the steward, who washed him clean with.turpentine, and no harm came of it. But Jack was afraid to come down until after he had passed two days in his lofty place of refuge. Hunger compelled him to descend. He chose a moment when I was sitting on deck, and, swing- ing himself down by a rope, he dropped suddenly into my lap, looking very sorry and seeming to ask me for pardon. I not only forgave him myself but-I procured his pardon from those in command. RUTH ASHWORTH.

div.head: MOTOR-CAR FATALITY.
div.p: MOTOR-CAR FATALITY.
Child Knocked Down by a Warrington Car.

The adjourned inquiry respecting the death of Thomas Cousins, the six-year-old son of Robert Cousins, timber labouter, Canal-view, Bootle, who was killed by being knocked down by a motor-car in Derby-road, Bootle, on Thursday last, was resumed at Bootle on Monday. The owner of the car, Mr. William Haddock Robinson, " The Mount," Warrington, was legally represented by Mr. T. S. Steel (Harrington), Mr. B. Quilliam appearing on behalf of the deceased's father. Mr. Robinson stated that he left Warrington at 2.30 on Friday for Liverpool, where he had some business to transact, and afterwards he found it necessary to go to Bootle. He was proceeding along Derby-road, near to the Borough Hospital, at a speed of between !lye and six miles an hour, when he saw three little boys stand- ing and talking on his left-hand side. On getting about six yards off them one of the lads left his friends and darted across the roadway. Witness saw it was no use sounding the born, and at once jammed on the' brakes. One of the splashboards of the car, however, just caught deceased, who was knocked down, the wheels passing over him. He was immediately picked up and carried to the hospital by a gentleman who witnessed the acci- dent, but the unfortunate boy succumbed to his injuries soon after admission. Previous to the accident witness sounded the horn on passing a street corner. He did everything he possibly could to avoid the mishap, and dislocated the machinery of the car through putting on ; the brakes. He had had experience in driving in the town, but had never driven in Booths before. A witness, named Owen, said the boy stepped off the parapet right in front of the car, which was travelling at a nominal speed. Coroner Brai:;hous3 observed there was no suggestion ;of careless driving. He knew there Wkls a prejudice against motors, but he did not think there might to be any prejudice, as motor cars had come to stay. There was the same danger with horses and traps. They were I very sorry Mr. Cousins, who was a widower, had lost his only son. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." On betpilf of his client, Mr. Steel expressed deep sympathy with the father, and said Mr. Robinson would undertake to defray all expenses in the matter.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING LAST NIGHT.

Public-House v. Shop Assessin3nts. A public meeting in support of the Licensing Bill was held in the Silver-street schools last evening. Councillor Wilkinson presided over a good attendance and was supported by Councillors Barton, Locker and Skelland, Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Messrs. C. E. Parker, E. Wynne-Jones, J. Ma,ginn, Farrar, G. Wallington, J. Morton. The CHAIRMA.N read a letter of apology for non- attendance from Mr. W. Clegg, who recalled the contest in Howley last November where " they mot the trade under the disguise of Christian guardian of the poor." Continuing, he said they were not met as temperance people, but as supporters of the Government. Of course they believed that the licensing Bill had for its object the promotion of temperance. Even those who were opposed to it had to admit the national evils that sprang from the excessive use of alcoholic drink, and said that something must be done to control the sale and manufacture of drink as was recommended by the Peel Commission. The Bill had been brought forward by the Liberal party as a fulfilment of its election pledges, and they welcomed it particularly on account of its democratic character. It restored to the magis- trates of Warrington the powers which should never have been taken horn them. (Applause). In the issue of new licences the public would hence- forth have a voice, and would be able to pre- vent the foisting upon a neighbourhood of a public-house which they did not desire. Councillor Wilkinson then referred to the matter of assessments pointing out that the introduction of the Licensing Bill had caused many people to think very deeply on that question. It would surprise his hearers if he told theca how high the assessments of shop property were in Warrington in comparison with the assessments of public-houses. Either the shop property was assessed I too high or the public-houses too low. They knew thej little shop kept for generations by the family of Mr. ' Richard Tort, tobacconist, in Hersemarket-street. That shop was paying as much in rates as the Griffin Hotel. (" Shame.") The Feathers Hotel in Bridge-street, a palatial building with a grand frontage, was assessed at about one half the amount paid by Atkinson's Cafe's Limited, in the same street. The Royal Copt Hotel was assessed at less than a shop like Boydell Bros'. He had a list of similar examples which he hoped would before long be placarded. (Hear, hear). The question would be gone into sooner or later, becasise it affected the rates and the rents. There was no need to run away with the idea that the closing of public-houses would be all loss to the brewers. The Corporation received £1.500 com- pensation in respect of the Queen's Hotel. AS a public- house that place brought them in £125 a year rental and carried an assessment of £lO6. To-day it was converted into two shops paying a rental of £l7O and an assess- ment of £145. The £1,500 was also bringing in 250 a year interest,so that the Corp &ration was receiving £220 a year instead of £125. It was computed that 2,000 publicans would be displaced by the operation of the Bill but as 7,000 publicans died annually there should be no difficulty in finding them fresh places. As to the complaint of local magnates that they would be ruined, it should be remembered that in le years there would be 60,000 licences. If the population increased in the same ratio as it had done during the past fourteen years and the temperance party could claim one half, be failed to see where the ruin would corns in. If he could persuade the brewing magnates in Warrington to deny themselves and invest one-half of their income for the current year, it would be sufficient to find old-age pensions of 10s. a week at the age of sixty for over 400 poor Warrington workingmen. (Applause.) How many of them would like to be in the same happy position of being ruined? He would not mind at all. (Applause.) I Mr. JOHN MAGINN said he was not a teetotaller and I did not come there to advocate rabid teetotalism, If the Bill had no other virtue, it was at least an attempt " to put an end to the monopoly of the brewer. (Applause.) They were told that beer would be dearer but did not commonsense tell them that monopolies were the cause of things being dearer not cheep? In England they had the dearest beer in the world in a Free Trade country. Why? Because it was one of the j few articles in England that was not sold under a system of free trade. The Bill was an effort to free the people from the power of an infernal monopoly. Absolute teetotalism was not what was needed in England, but a good beverage that was a thirst quencher, and not the terrible intoxicant that was forced on them to-clay. The brewers could sell what quality of beer they liked at their own prices and it was no wonder that drunkenness increased. With regard to investors, the majority in any country should not suffer for the minority. They had nothing to do witiz those people investing money in breweries and why should they be forced to finance them for a bad speculation? Mr. Maginn then dealt at some length with the evils of the tied house system and also alluded to the question of assessments. He also instanced the case of the Feathers' Hotel end Atkinson's Cafe, pointing out that the hotel was sold for £4,800 and had a frontage of 16 yards. Atkinson's Cafe cost between £1,500 and £1,600, had a frontage of 51 yards and stocd on a fourth of the land occupied by the hotel. Yet the hotel paid on a rateable value of £76 loa and the care on £l3O 10s. ("Shame.") The Assessment Committee was composed of twelve gentlemen, including two publicans and one brewer. , The Cereenetee read a telegram from Mr. George Walker regretting that he was unable to attend as he was detained in Manchester. Mr. E. WYNNE JONES said the drink traffic at the present time stood in the way of all true and effective social reform. This was the third attempt the Liberals had made to deal with the question and the third attempt was going to pay for all. (Applause.) The Bill was going through this time, but even if they were defeated it would be far better to be beaten in an attempt to make England honest and sober than to cling to office like Mr. Balfour dbcl long after his welcome had passed. (Applause.) The brewers bad miscalculated the forces that were behind the j3ill. All that was noblest and best in the country was rallying to its support. (Applause.) They had to break the power ,of the drink traffic or temperance and social reform would be set back for a generation. I The Bill was not based on the proposals of I extreme teetotallers but largely on the proposals of the brewers themselves and of the Church of England Temperance Society. The brewers opposed it not because of the higher licence duties or because it would or would not make for tempesince reforin, but because they knew that the tied-house system with its unfair agreements, with its bad and adultrated driuks, would be revolutionised. The Bill had been rightly described as the Magna Chaste of the tied house tenant and the honest publican had nothing to fear from it. (Applause.) The brewers had taken out of the pockets of the tied house tenants for the last twelve years something like 13 millions a year in unfair profits. The trade was the worst employer of labour of all, spending less in pro- portion to capital than any other trade in the country. (Applause.) The Labour party was solidly with the Government in support of the Bill. (A Voice : Is Victor Grayson with you?) Well, he was all by him- self. (Laughter and applause.) The forces of the trade were skilfully and powerfully organized and the friends of progress must make up their minds to carry the measure at all costs. (Applause). Councillor BARTON moved the following resolution : "That this meeting heartily welcomes the Licensing Bill introduced into the HOMO of Commons by the Prime Minister and pledges it 3 strenous support to the t Government vierncm. Een.tpi,ntncKarErny:ning stehceoßndililnign,tsoaildawt.h when the. Bill was introduced the other side said at once that the Liberal Party had committed suicide, and there were great rejoiciegs and fireworks in this town. (Laughter.) Now, however, they all realized that the Bill was winning its way on its own merits—(hear, hear)— because people who got their knowledge from the Bill itself and not from the posters on the public- houses recognised that it was a fair, temperate, and just Bill. (Applause.) The question of assessments was a grave one affecting the interests of every ratepayer in the town. The difficulty ought not to be a great one for under the new Bill compensation for closed houses would be based on the assessment. They would there- fore have the curious spectacle in Warrington of the brewers who had for years done all they could to depress the assessmonts,now trying to lift them as high as possible so that the compensation would be proportiouately high. (Applause.) The Rev. C. II kIIVEY COOK supported. The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried with two dissentients. "The Widow and Orphan."

Chancellor's Offer to the Brewers. Mr. Alex Ure, M.P., Solicitor General for Scotland spoke at a mass meeting at Skipton on Saturday night, under the chairmanship of Mr. NV. Clough? Liberal member for the Skipton division. Commenting upon the Licensing Bill Mr. lire said temperance reformers looked upon it as the longest stride in the direction of temperance reform that most of them had ever seen, and it was the most the Government could do in the present state of public opinion in England and \Vales. Amid loud cheers he continued: " I dare the House of Lords to reject this bill." He denied that the passing of the measure would bring the financial ruin in its wake which was predicted by the brewers, and in refusing the plea that the widow and orphan would suffer announced an offer which was authorised by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It was this : If the great brewers and distillers will pay every widow and orphan every penny they have lost in the liquor trade before the 27th of February last, when the bill was introduced, the Chancellor of the Exchequer will pay every widow and orphan every penny they have lost since the day the bill saw the light.— (Laughter and applause). A resolution supporting the bill was passed, with only ens dissentient. Meeting at Wycliffe Church. -•-• in sf the Licensi

div.head: Voice From California. Mr. H Whitham on the Bill.
div.p: A Voice From California. Mr. H Whitham on the Bill.

Dear Sir, —I have just received my "Examiner " and 1 I feel I must write to say how pleased lam with the ' attitude the people seem to be taking on the beer question. As a temperance man and more especially as a Socialist I aria sure no real progress will ever be made until the working man is made to see that only by way of sobriety can he ever become a thoughtful man. Drunkenness, as an outcome, mainly, of temptation, is the greatest obstacle to Socialism and if the Christian knows only the letter of the Lord's prayer and knows not its spirit why the Socialist should say firmly " thou shall not lead In into temptation," and so teach he of Wilderspool and also he of Trinity Church the ethics of their own religion. I served my apprenticeship at Rylands Bros. anti I could name quite a number of young men who at that time were completely ruined by tie tempter having placed not less than half-a-dozen of these baits for the feeble minded close to the mill gates. I could refer to a number of names but what's the use?

The Rev. T. ltlrte.En speaking at the Bold-street school said something that is worth repeating : " Why are the Brewers afraid? Simply because Mel] cannot trust the people. The Government Bill was moderate, clear, and perfectly just. It was not the working man the Brewers cared for ; it was laterest and dividends. With them the rights of property were more sacred than the rights of man or God. The saddest feature as far as Warrington , was concerned was that the Drink Trade was ao ; great a supporter of the Church that the clergy were found on the side of a demoralising trade and against social reform." That's it. Neither the brewers nor yet the clergy trust the people. The Church of Eegland depends to a largo extent on the guzzling capacity of the workers. I see Lady Greenall accompanied her husband to a Crewe meeting, and the good lady "supported " her I husband on the trying occasion. Does the good lady I know that what they At and what they drink and what I they put on their backs is timply the sweat of the slums. I There are two features about this drink question ' that should not be lost sight of. The Government measure is not a teetotal Bill. It simply is an effort to remove a little of the temptation away from the work- man's track. Canterbury has 150 "pubs." In the near future there will be 50. Can anyone say how it happens that the cathedral towns of England, the homes of the Bishops, are the highest in their percentage of over- licensing ? Strange there should be such a close relationship between church and "pub." Possibly the course the Primate is taking may end this. This ques- tion of thepub" is note political one nor yet a religious one. It is more than either. It is a moral question. Note the case of J. Harris, Winwick-road, who is now I serving six months with hard labour. His home was a drinking den. On frequent occasions prisoner, his wife land other men and women had b3en found in a drunken condition, and despite frequent warnings no effort had been made to improve. The children were neglected, and were scantily clothed. The bedding was filthy, and the conditions under which the children lived were injurious to their health. Would Lady Greens:ll and her friends like to live in homes of this sort ? Does she know the stuff that makes these homes is made by the Brewer of Wildeespool ? I hope most sincerely that the Bill will become law. H. WHITHAINI.
Alameda, California. ---.2.----

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY GOLF. Mr. A. H. CrosfielTbiats Dr. Macnamara.
div.p: PARLIAMENTARY GOLF. Mr. A. H. CrosfielTbiats Dr. Macnamara.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., played in the Parlia- mentary Golf Handicap which opened at the Cinque Port Club Links, Deal, on Saturday... In the first round he 'beat Mr. S. Robinson, M.P., by 2 holes and in the second round he defeated Mr. J. W. Wilson, ' MP., by 2 and 1. The "Manchester Guardian " London correspondent writes: —The most remarkable feature of Saturday's play in the first two rounds of the Parliamentary golf handicap was the success of the short-handicap players. The average handicap of the thirty-two competitors now left in is about ten, and at fourth of them have allowances of four or loss. Parliament could not put a much better team in the field than Mr. 11. W. Forster, Mr. Frank Newnes, Mr. A. J. Robertson, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, Mr. A. Lyttleton, Mr. A. H. Crosfielcl, Mr. H. J. B3deley, and Mr. Mitchell Thompson. Seven of these eight have qualified for the third round, and Mr. Mitchell I Thompson was beaten after a very hard match with Mr. Forster. Winners of previous years who are still in the running are Mr. Newnes, Mr. Robertson, and Mr. Badeley. Mr. Bonar Law, last year's winner, and Mr. Balfour have both been defeated. As usual, Mr. Balfour had almost all the spectators following his match. Mr. R. Pearce scored a popular victory. If their numbers grow as they are growing now, Parliamentary golfers will soon find in the Daylight- Saving Bill their only hope of getting through two rounds in a day. THE TITIRD ROUND.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. (handicap 3), defeated Dr. Macnamara, M.P. (handicap 10), by 2 boles in the third round of the Parliamentary Handicap at Mitcham yesterday morning. Mr. 11. W. Forster, M.P. (plus :3) beat Mr. C. W. Cimpioa,examiner,House of Commons (9) by 2 and 1.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
To-day's Great Event. '

To-day the first Warrington Musical Festival will be held in the Parr Hall and there is every indication that it will be a great success. Over 1,000 competitors have entered and with such an array of talent a musical treat may be confidently anticipated. The afternoon concert at 2 o'clock will be presided over by the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) and the chief attraction will be the competition for male choirs, in which the entries include the famous Manchester Orpheus Choir. The test piece is " King of Worlds" (David Jamin). Another most interesting item will be the children's choral competition for which five choirs have entered, including the Beamont Council School, Warrington, and the Warrington Band of Hope Union ,select choir. The pieces chosen are "Whispering Wind " (Labbett) and " Oft, in the stilly night" (Mc Naught). The prizes will be distri- buted by the Mayoress. The evening concert will com- mence at 0 30, and Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. will take the chair. The programme will include the great event of the day —the chief choral competition for mired choirs. Eight leading choirs have entered and the test pieces are "He,watching over Israel"(Mendelssohn)and " Moonlight " (Eaton Failing). The valuable challenge shield will be presented to the winners by Mrs. A. H. Crosaeld. At the close of the contest the massed choirs will sing the test pieces uuder the conductor- ship of Dr. IV. CT'. McNaught. Another event in which great interest is being taken is the Church or Chapel Choir competition, in which four local choirs will take part. The test piece is " Abide with me" (Dunstan). Mrs. James Hyl:l3 will present the winning choir with the silver cup. At each concert there will be a song by Miss Frances A.ndrews (con- tralto) .and a violiu solo by Mks 80/Ashcan Wool. Dr. W. G. McNaught and Mr. Wilfred Jones, HA.11., Iwill be the adjudicators.
