div.head: MEETING AT SANKEY.
div.p: MEETING AT SANKEY.
STIRRING SPEECH BY MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P. •
Mr. James Dodds and Colonel Hall Walker's Lament.

A highly successful meeting in support of the Licens- ing Bill was held in Sankey Sunday School on Monday evening. Thera was a large and enthusiastic audience and, with the exception of a handful of opponents, feel- ing was entirely in favour of th 9 Government measure. Mr. James Dodds presided and was supported on the platform by Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.' P. the Revs. A. M. Mitchell (Vicar of Burtonwood), C. Harvey Cook and E. J. Gawne, Messrs. C. E. Parker, G. Faulkner, T. Haley and E. Marshall. THE CHAIRMAN AND COLONEL HALL WALKER'S LAMENT. -

The CH tIEMIN said he did not know ender whose auspices the meeting had been convened, but when he was asked to preside he willingly consented because he believed that the Licensing Bill was the finest measure that had been brought before the people of this country in this age. (Applause.) Certainly it was the best Bill that he bad known in his time and he had watched pretty keenly the party politics of this country for fifty years. They were not met, continued Mr. Dodds, to abuse anybody. He believed there were amongst the brewers and the publicans good men who were anxious to do what was right and to help their fellowmen. The trade was a legitimate one, but his contention was that n'o interest, however important and however strong, had a right to put itself in a position of antagonism to the great body of the people. (Applause.) A trade which caused so much misery, poverty and crime as the drink traffic ought to be under the control of the nation through the legislature. In view of the disastrous results of the trade, and of the fact that for four hundred years the law of tho land had been absolutely clear that licences were issued for one year end no longer, and seeing that that right was taken away without any mandate from the people, the nation now had a right to step in, especially as the great majority of their representatives in the present Parliament were sent to Westminster pledged to support a measure of Licensing Reform such as the one which was now before the country. (Applause). First of all the people Must get back the control of the licences. They must stand firmly for that ; without it they might as well do nothing. The control belonged to them with- out a doubeas was proved by cases in the Law Courts, by the Over Darwen and Sharpy Wakefield decisions. The brewers, thinking the power to close houses wculd not be used, began to get bold of all the licences they could, purchasing them recklessly at excessive Prices, with the result that in 1001 something had to be done as the magistrates *ld not care to act under tho con- dition of things brought about by that buying up of licences. Mr. Asquith's Bill was not robbery ; it was AI ERE RESTITUTION. It was giving back to the people the right which was filched from them and it should be borne in mind that Mr. Balfour's Government was told that whenever the Liberals got in power they would undo the 1904 Act. Mr. Balfour said there was nothing in his Bill to pre- vent the legislature at any future time stepping in and putting on a time limit or undoing all that the Act of 1901 did. Lord Hugh Cecil definitely pit it to the Government on June 6th, 1901, that that was so, and Mr. Balfour agreed that it was. The present Government therefore was not doing anything it had not a perfect right to do in seeking to bring about the condition of things which obtained prior to the Act of 1901. There must be a time limit. (Applause.) Soon after the introduction of the present measure be (Mr. Dodds) said the fight would be not as to the length of the time limit but as to whether there should be a time limit at all, and events had proved that to be the case. The brewers were standing out against any time limit what- ger, and on that point temperance reformers mast join issate. (Applause.) Another good feature of tte measure was the granting of local option, so that the people in their respective districts should decide whether a public house should be thrust upon them or cot. He had been reading some remarks made the other day by COLONEL HALL WALKER, the representative of an adjoining constituency, who told them of the dire consequences which would follow the passing of the Bill. "If the Bill passed into law," said Colonel Hall Walker " he should cease to be their member. He would probably have to sell everything he possessed and start afresh in life, and that after thirty years of constant toil, some given to the State, a good deal to local affairs, public, private, and charit- able." (Laughter.) That was indeed a very gloomy out- look, and he (Mr. Dodds) felt curious as to whether from the position of the company with which Colonel Hall Walker was associated as a director, there was any chance of the Colonel having anything left if the Bill passed. (Laughter.) He had before him the balance sheet of Messrs. Walker's concern which included three com- panies—two property companies and one brewing com- pany. The profits for 1907 amounted to £323.461 2s. Bd. and the balance brought forward from the previous year was £16,905. After paying the directors' and auditors' fees which amounted to £15,203, there remained £323,153 for distribution. Of that slim £231,050 was divided amongst the shareholders, £74,000 was placed to the reserve fund and £22,508 14s. 7d. was carried forward to next year. This company could not he complained of very much in regard to the way in which it treated the widows and orphans who had sleares in it. He was told on good authority that the ordinary shares were held by the members of the Walker family them- selves and those shares, of course, got the biggest plums. The debenture and preference shares were the only ones that the widows and orphans could hold and before they could be touched the million canital of the ordinary shareholders would have to be lord, as well as the reserve fund of £195,000 and the £74,00e just added to it. lie (Mr. Dodds) had always said that the brewery trade was so good on the whole that in the good com- panies the brewers would see to it that the widows and orphans had to take shares with fixed dividends while they themselves received the big plums in the shape of the dividends which accrued on the ordinary or deferred ahares.Tlie ordinary shares in Messrs. Walker's paid 10 per cent. so that last year £lOO,OOO was divided amongst the members of the Walker family ancl friends, who held the ordinary shares in the concern. He did not know what proportion of that sum Colonel flail Walker would receive but he felt that if the Bill passed and two-thirds of the houses were allowed to remain, the member for Widnes would hardly came to the sad condition which be pictured in his speech. (Laughter.) Ridiculous allegations were made in regard to the unemployment which would be created by the closing of public-houses, but he would not deal with that question as it was fully gone into by Mr. C. E. Parker in the letter in which he pulverised Mr. W. P. ltylands in Saturday's papers. (Laughter and applause). , THE CHURCH NO LONGER TIED. The Rev. A. M. MlTcfmr, moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting heartily welcomes the Licensing Bill now before Parliament as a substantial measure of temperance reform, reducing excessive drinking facilities, and securing to the people the ultimate control of the liquor traffic, and trusts that more stringent regulations will he made in regard to drinking clubs ; and further calls upon all citizens to unite in th:s national effort to diminish the gigantic evils produced by the present licensing system." He con. gratulated the Newton division upon being represented by a total abstainer and one who was thoroughly sound and whole-hearted in the matter of the Licensing Bill. No doubt Mr. Seddon had heard about his naughtiness— (laughter)—but whit he lost now, if he was losing any- thing, he would gain a hundred fold by and by and ha (Mr. Mitchell) hoped, in fact he felt sure that he would stand to his guns. (Applause.) One of the happiest things in connection with the Licensing Bill was the noble front which had been presented by the Labour smembers.(Applause.) The magnificent majority obtained on the second reading was very largely due to their attitude. The Solicitor General well said : The brewer may tie the public house but he cannot tie the House of Commons." (Applause.) There was another body which refused to be tied any longer by the drink traffic, and that was the Church. (Applane.) He knew there were individual towns. and parishes which were

-- --- still tied to the brewer. There was one not auite so far away as Burton-on-Trent (Laughter) and that town was not Buttonwood. (Laughter.) He hoped that town would presently come to a better mind and show itself to be sane like other towns and parishes on the matter of tho Bill. The Church was no longer tied to the brewer—and he thanked God for their free- -dom, fie was glad also to note that the Bishop of ,
WARRINGTON FOOTBALL
CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING. The "Spirit of Politics."

There was a largo attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club, which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street, on 'Thursday evening. Mr. J. H. Warren (president) presided, and was sup- ported by Mr. Henry Ashton (secretary), Mr. T. Pemberton (treasurer) and members of the committee. REPORTS AND BALANCE SHEET.

Mr. E. A. SANDERS moved the adoption of the Secre- tary's and Treasurer's reports and balance sheet, which were summarised in last week's "Examiner." Mr. OSBORNM seconded and the motion was unani- mously agreed to without comment. RETIRING PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS. "THE SPIRIT OF POLITICS." The CITAIRMAN then moved the election of Alderman D. Tinnion as president of the club. He observed that he had known the Alderman for something like thirty years. He (Mr. Warren) had at home a record of the minutes of a meeting of the warrington Football Club held in 1378 at the Patten Arms Hotel, and he believed Alder nan Tinnion's name was mentioned as being elected to the committee. He had taken a very keen interest in football from that day to this. He was one of the oldest members of the club —in fact he believed the Alderman was the oldest continuously paying member. As a player himself he knew what the game was as well as any of them and he had always kept in touch with it, and his services on that ground alone must be of great value to ' the club because judgment was required in selecting players. Alderman Tinnion's position in the town was well known. He had worked his way up to a place of very high honour and he (Mr. Warren) hoped to see him some day attain the highest civic) honour which Warrington could confer upon any of her sons. (Applause.) His business acumen also fitted him for the presidency of that club because, after all, the club could not be governed entirely by footballers but there must be talented businessmen at the head to make it a success. With that trinity of qualifications he was sure they could not do bettor than elect Alderman Tinnion as their president. (Applause.) At the beginning of last season, continued Mr. Warren, they set out with great determination to win the League Championship. They thought they had won the cup so often that they would pay particular attention to the league. It was, however, a case of" Man proposes, but God disposes." Unfortunately although at one time they had the best team they ever had—a team equal to any in the Uniu when they were all playing at their best_ —they had so many cripples at critical moments that it was no wonder they came down to the seventh place instead of being in the first four. At the last annual meeting he .mentioned the question of amalgamation with the Rugby Union. It was laugh- able to think about it now. They thought twelve months ago that an amalgamation with the Rugby Union tyould have been a good thing. Where was the Rugby Union now? The Northern Union was sweep- ing the decks. So far away as New Zealand and Australia they were capturing the game. He (Mr. Warren) went to Tony Pandy, at the invitation of the Committee, to see the game between England and %Vales and the enthusiasm manifested and the eulogistic manner in whidh the game was spoken of convinced him that in twelve months the whole of South Wales would be with them—(applause)—and possibly before another four or five years were over the whole of England and Wales would be with them, with the exception probably of the public schools. (Applause.) A matter which he regretted was that during the last year or two there had been a spirit of politics introduced into the club. It was very reprehensible and he hoped, without going into details as many members present knew what he meant, that it would not be pushed any further. The club had not been a political affair and he hoped it never would be. (Hear, hear.) They ran the club for professional sport and they did not want politics to interfere with them in any sense of the word. He hoped the members would knock back anything of the kind very strongly. The committee he had had to work with was a splendid one and he could not quite see how it was that there was such a rush of men to get on the committee because he could assure them it entailed a great deal of hard work and a number of qualifications. He would point out to the meeting that those who whaled to support a new nominee might by plumping for their own man knock the best man off the committee through abstaining to vote for him in the belief that he was certain to be elected. If they thought any member of the committee was not qualified and wiehed to substitute somebody else, it would only be manly to tell him his faults and give him a chance of defending himself. (Applause.) Mr. Warren then alluded to the unfortunate and untimely death of Mr. J. T. (" Testi ") Thorniley and said he was sure he was voicing the feel- ings of everyone present when he said their sympathy went out in a most whole-hearted manner to the widow and children. (Hear, hear.) He must in conclusion thank the club and in particular the members of the committee for the very courteous manner in which they had dealt with him throughout his terra of &lice. He hoped to be able to help them and take part in their battles as a spectator for many years to come. (Applause.) Mr. JAMES CRETCULEY seconded, and said he had known Alderman Tinnion as long as anyone in the room who had played football. Alderman Tinnion played with the Warrington Zingari Club which became the Warrington Football Club and ever since then he had been a paying member. (Applause). The resolution was then put to the meeting and enthusiastically carried. NEW PRESIDENT'S SPEECH.

Alderman TnisiroN then took the chair. He thanked Mr. Warren for the very fulsome way in which he had proposed his election to the presidency. He only wished he deserved all he had said and he hoped that at the end of the year when he vacated the office he would be as entitled to the praise and approbation of the members as he was on taking the chair for the first time that night. (Applause). He also thanked the members for the hearty reception they had accorded him. They had certainly given him encouragement to commence the duties of the presidency and he hoped their confidence would not be reposed in vain. He had been a member of the various associations and clubs which had played the Rugby code in Warrington for considerably over a quarter of a century and he had always had a very warm and kind regard for the Warrington Football Club. He had rejoiced with them in their joys and sympathised with them in their sorrows and he felt exceedingly proud of the position he occupied that night. His only regret was that he had to displace his friend Mr. Warren who had filled the office so ably in the past. As, however,it was an honour that should go round, he (Alderman Tinnion) could not grumble. He felt that except for very special reasons no one should hold the presidency for more than one year because he was sure there was not a member of the club or a gentleman within a radius of ten miles of Market-gate who would not be as proud as he was to occupy that position. They had an excellent football club in Warrington in almost every respect. In the first place the club had a high reputation. They had a good ground as far as the playing patch was conmrned and ' ho was sorry the part allotted to the spectators was so limited. Apart from that he believed they had the best turf in Lancashire—be was going to say in England (Applause.) They had always had a very excellent style of play in Warrington. He knew something about it and he considered that the high standard of football displayed by their club was second to none in the country. (Applause.) Their players wen men who played the game and he thought that in that respect they had very few equals. They had also a great advantage in the officials of the club. Officials and members of other clubs in the. Northern Union had told them that they
Hewitt, T. Locker, W. Chalmers and F. Barber (retiring committee); T. Barnes, jun., T. P. Bradshaw, H.Rogers• J. Sadlow.

_ Mr. ASHTON said the committee regretted to have to introduce a discordant note in such a harmonious meet- ing, but he had to call attention to the nomination of Mr. H. Rogers. The member whose name appeared as seconder had told him that he had not signed his name. He, however, gave Mr. Rogers permission to write it; he was present when it was signed and made his mark, but that mark was not witnessed by anybody. He (Mr. Ashton) did not think that was the proper way to do , business. Mr. Ashton emphasised the responsibility I which would rest upon the new committee as the lease ; of the ground would shortly expire and the guarantee I would have to be renewed. The CHAIRMAN said he was prepared to leave the ; meeting to judge as to the validity of Mr. Roger's ' nomination, but he should certainly advise that it was not in order. The MEMBER whose name appeared as seconder explained that be could write but he gave Mr. Rogers permission to write his name, as it was very dark and he had not his spectacles with him. He attached his mark to the signature. The CHAIRMAN : That is not a nomination. We want to have these things straight and above board. Mr. ROGERS said there appeared to be certain oppo- sition to him by the Secretary and he did not kuow ; why. He would, however, withdraw his name from the nominations.

The CIIA.IRMAN : I think you are well advised in doing so. The ballot resulted as follows :—F. Barber 271, T. Bowers 265, T. Locker 249. W. Hewitt 239, W. Chalmers 216, T. Davies ISt, T. Barnes, jun., 126, J. Sudlow 89, T. P. Bradshaw 55. The retiring committee were therefore re-elected. THE LATE MR. J. T. THORNILEY.

The CHAIRIIAN read a letter from Mr. Sam Oddy asking the club to joßti with the workmates of the late Mr. J. Thorniley in raising 9, fund for the benefit of the widow and seven children of the late Mr. J. T. Thorniley who have been left but scantily provided for. On the motion of the PRESIDENT seconded by Mr. S. W. JEFFREY a vote of condolence was passed with the widow and family, all the members standing. Mr. S. V. JEFFERY then moved that the Committee be empowered to make a generous contribution to the fund. He did not look upon it as charity, as the valu- able services which" Tos'n rendered to the club in the old days demanded recognition. He did not benefit as many players benefited cow awl as there were on the committee old fellow-players of his, the amount might safely be left to their discretion. . .

Mr. S. WRIonT seconded and said there was no greater football enthusiast than "Tosh." He not only played but paid to play. Mr. E. A. SANDERS in supporting suggested that in addition to the donation from the club funds each member of the club should contribute an extra 6d. when be paid his annual subscription and that would mean another £25. The resolution was unanimously carried. SPECIAL RESG.LUTION.—COMMITTEE CRITICISED. The following special resolution appeared on the agenda : —That at any time on a rovisition stating the business, and signed by one tenth of the members of tho Club, the secretary shall convene a Special General Meeting, which shall take place within 10 days after the requisition is in his hands. In answer to Mr. S. Wright, the SECRETARY admitt ed that the resolution was not proposed and seconded as provided by the rules, but the cohimittee had placed it on the agenda. The CHAIRMAN ruled that it was proper business be be discussed.

Mr. JEFFERY : What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, and if rules are made they should be kept. The SECRETARY explained that at present a requisi- tion for a special meeting had only to be signed by 20 members. The rule, however, was made when the club had only 200 members, and the time had come when it should be altered in proportion to the growth of the club. Mr. BURDETT seconded. Mr. S. WRIGHT contended that the alteration would curtail the privileges of the members. The rule had never been abused to his knowledge, and it seemed to him that because the members a short time ago decided on a certain course which was perhaps not acceptable to the committee, the alteration was proposed to pre- vent a repetition of it. It would be very difficult to obtain 100 signatures. .

After furtlier discussion it was decided, on the pro- position of Mr. S. W. JEFFERY, seconded by Mr. E. V. WA.LICER, that the number of signatures required for tt requisition should be fifty. TRUSTEES.
Messrs. T. Bowers and T. Locker were re-elected trust ees.

HONORARIUMS. The meeting approved the granting of honorariums of ,C 33 to the Secretary, £l5 to the treasurer, and each to the auditors. VOTES OF THANKS. Mr. E, ENGLAND moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Warren for his services as President. He expressed hi% great disappointment that at least-, one cup had not come to Warrington during the past season. He could Only put it down to lack of earnestness or of training - that the team did not defeat Wakefield Trinity at London. The Ciummax seconded and the vote was heartily I passed. A similar compliment to the Chairman for presiding concluded the meeting.

div.head: BIG GAS PROFITS. Cheering News for the Ratepayers.
div.p: BIG GAS PROFITS. Cheering News for the Ratepayers.

The balance sheet of the Corporation Gas Depart- ment .was submitted to the Gas Committee yesterday morning, and disclosed unexpectedly good results from the trading of the year ending March 21st last; The gross profits amounted to the unprecedented tots/ of £23,800 12s. 3d. After paying interest and sinking fund charges, the net balance amounts to £15,59'3' 19s. 11d. The increased production of gas during the year amounts to nearly 23 million cubic feet. The figures establish a record all round for the Depart' m9nt. It will be remembered that at the Budget meeting of the Council a month ago, the aura .0f £11,500 was guaranteed from the gas profits in relief 'of the rates. Seeing that the profits are so higher than was expected, it is possible that a still Ilarger sum will be available.

div.p: PRESENTATION TO CANON PENRHYN,
Fifty-six Years in Orders.

Churchpeople in the diocese of Liverpool have Well shown their affection and esteem for the senior cauorl of Liverpool (Canon Penrhyn, M.A.) by joining cod heartily with his parishioners of Winwick, who yester- day presented to Canon Penrhyn his portrait in 005 nod an illuminated address, on his attaining eight) years of age and fifty-six years in holy orders. The picture was painted by Mr. F. T. Copnall, of Liverpool. The rev. gentleman is depicted against ,5 dark, plain background; the position is easy, unaffectear and natural. Canon Penrhyn is the second son of Mr. EriWarct ILeycester Penrhyn, J.P., DL., and of lady Eliaabethr eldest daughter of the thirteenth Earl of Derby. E 0 i 9 a scion of two ancient families—the Stanleys and tb„9 Leycesters of Toft, Cheshire. He was educated at and Balliol College, Oxford, and was ordained in 18afl; With the exception of the first four years of clerica' life, he has bean wholly in Lancashire. He was curate, at Winwick 1856-8, Bickerstaffe 1151-9, and vicar 01- linyton 1819-90. He was in 1.110 one of the Mel clergymen choses by the first Bishop of Liyerpo°o (the late Dr. Ryle) to be honorary canons of Or newly-founded bishopric. In 1590 he became rector 0!. Winwick in succession to his uncle, the Into 0011 Hopwood. He has been Proctor for the Archdeacoor:6, ,of Warrington in York Convocation since 1857 . if Rural Dean of Winwick, chaplain to the TlishoP 01 Liverpool, one of the secretaries of LiverPoa,i , Cathedral Committee, and senior governor of Rossal' School. Despite his advanced age, the canon is vellir active, a great traveller, and retains keen interest 1,, 1 cricket, a sport in which be formerly excelled. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE YOUNG LIBERALS. Meetings at Liverpool. Delegates from all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire assembled in the Abercomby Reform Club, Hope-street, Liverpool, on Saturday afternoon, in connection with the quarterly council meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of the National League of Young Liberals. The federation is still in its infancy, but there are already twenty-five leagues affiliated with it in Lancashire and Cheshire, with a membership of over 2,000. In the absence of thtt president, Mr. C. Williams (Stockport), the chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Ainsworth, of the Liverpool branch, one of the vice-presidents of the federation. Mr. F. Godwin Lloyd (hon. secretary) reported that the whole of the constitution of the federation had now been decided, and the council was invited to take steps to strengthen and spread the league. It was suggested that efforts should be made to establish branches at Hyde, Preston, Todmorden, Alderley, St. Helens, and Southport, and to strengthen the branches at Littleborough and Heywood. A sub- committee was appointed to initiate the work, and branches in adjoining districts were asked to co-operate. On the proposition of Mr. Battle (Bolton), seconded by IMr. Hellawell (Stockport), it was resolved that the league should devote itself to practical politics, and by co-operating with and assisting the official Liberal party do all in its power to enable the policy of the Government to be better known I and more thoroughly nmierstood. With the view of 'assisting branches to obtain competent speakers on political topics, it was decided to draw up a speakers' list, each branch being asked to send in the names of I available speakers. Suggestions were made for active I propaganda work during the summer months by open- air meetings. The Central Council was invited to hold its July meeting at either Chester or Southport. An radjournment was made for tea, and a successful open- air meeting was subsequently held at the Wellington Monument. Mr. R. H. Tattersall (Birkenhead) presided, and speeches in support of the Government and advo- cating further measures of social reform were delivered by Mr. Hawthorn (Warrington), Mr. Battle (Bolton), Mr. Lloyd (Manchester), and other delegates. DEATH OF MR. LAURENCE SCOTT. We regrst to announce the death of Mr. Laurence Prestwich Scott, eldest son of Mr. C. P. Scott, of The Firs, Fallowfield. He was a member of the editorial staff of the " Manchester Guardian," to which he had contributed many authoritative articles, chiefly on art, drama, and literature. After leaving Corpus Christi, Oxford, he continued his studies in Paris, and subse- quently he had editorial charge of the book reviews in the " Manchester Guardian." Ile was only 30 years of age._
